1021-the-congo-and-other-poems:
Vachel Lindsay, an American poet who read his verse aloud on the road, fills this book with chants meant to be heard, not just read on the page. Its best-known piece, "The Congo," beats out drums, chants, and crowd noise to tell of Africa as seen through American fancy. Other poems praise small towns, heroes, and the open road.

Lindsay wrote for plain folk and sang his lines with a performer's verve, which made him a popular voice in his day. The poems mix praise, satire, and gospel fire. Read now, the title poem also shows the limits of its age, and the book stands as a loud, odd, and vivid piece of early American verse.
1031-charmides-and-other-poems:
Oscar Wilde, still a young Oxford man, opens this early book with "Charmides," a lush retelling of a Greek myth, and follows it with lyrics on art, love, Rome, and the sea. The poems show a student drunk on beauty, keen to prove himself in the high style of Keats and the classics.

Gods, statues, flowers, and tombs crowd the lines, and the verse aims for rich sound and fine finish over plain sense. Some pieces already carry Wilde's wit and polish. The book marks the start of a career that would soon move from verse to plays and prose, and it pleases readers who love ornate late Victorian song.
1034-poems:
Wilfred Owen, a young English officer killed a week before the Armistice in 1918, left behind the fiercest poems of the First World War. His lines put readers in the trench: gas, mud, rotting feet, and boys sent to die for old lies about glory. The poems were gathered after his death by friends.

Owen's pity runs through every page, but so does his anger at generals, priests, and poets who praised war from afar. Images of blinded men and wasted youth still hit hard. The book made him the voice of his generation's loss, and it stands at the heart of English war poetry.
1042-a-reading-of-life-with-other-poems:
George Meredith, the Victorian novelist turned poet, reads human life as a choice between ease and effort in the title sequence of this 1901 book. Short lyrics weigh manhood, love, and fate, while a second part turns Homer's Iliad into English hexameters, with Achilles raging and armies massing.

Meredith's verse is dense and aphoristic, packed with nature images and hard-won maxims. He urges readers to face pain and grow, not to drift. The book shows his late style at full stretch, and it appeals to readers who like poetry that thinks as hard as it sings.
109-renascence-and-other-poems:
Edna St. Vincent Millay's first book announces a voice both tender and defiant. Renascence and Other Poems opens with the title poem, in which the speaker's soul swells beyond the world and returns chastened. Short lyrics on love, sorrow, and the hills follow.

Poems like Interim, The Suicide, God's World, and Afternoon on a Hill show Millay's range in few lines. Sonnets close the volume with formal control and feeling. The book made the young poet famous before she turned twenty-five. It remains a bright entry point to her work.
1186-poems:
Alice Meynell, a Victorian poet of fine and Catholic sensibility, gathers lyrics on love, loss, nature, and faith in this 1903 volume. Sonnets to the beloved, songs of spring, and laments for the dead show her craft: short lines, clear images, and a grave, musical tone.

Meynell writes with restraint, letting a single image carry a poem's feeling. Her work won praise from poets who prized finish over noise. The book gives a compact view of a respected minor poet, and it suits readers who like quiet, polished verse. Meynell's restraint and clear images give the volume its lasting charm.
1439-dreams:
Olive Schreiner's Dreams is a small book of allegories, printed in the order she wrote them. Each dream is a short parable. A hunter seeks truth, a woman stands at a gate, and a soul walks a road, all told in plain, biblical language that lets the image carry the meaning.

The pieces speak for women's freedom, for labour, and for a faith that must be lived rather than recited. Schreiner dedicated the book to a small girl-child who might one day grasp what her age could only glimpse. It is a brief, earnest work of vision, still fresh in its hope.
1469-poems:
Francis Thompson's Poems, in the 1909 Burns and Oates edition, gather the lyrics that made his name, including the love lyrics grouped as Love in Dian's Lap. Before Her Portrait in Youth and A Carrier-Song show his musical, image-rich manner, and later pieces turn from earthly beauty toward faith.

Thompson, a Catholic poet of the late Victorian age, writes of love, faith, and the divine pursued through earthly beauty. His diction is lush and his rhythms are bold. The volume is a good introduction to a poet once ranked among the finest lyric voices of his generation.
1471-new-poems:
Francis Thompson's New Poems, in its third English edition of 1907, gathers later lyrics headed by Sight and Insight, including The Mistress of Vision, Contemplation, and The Dread of Height. A dedication opens the book, and the poems that follow pursue vision, law, and the soul's ascent with Thompson's characteristic music.

The verse is dense with image and Catholic feeling, and its rhythms carry readers through long, meditative lines. Thompson's health was failing, and the book has a valedictory air. It is a rewarding volume for readers who already love his earlier lyrics and want his mature voice.
1567-poems:
T. S. Eliot's Poems of 1920, published by Alfred A. Knopf and dedicated to Jean Verdenal, gather his early lyrics after Prufrock. Gerontion opens the book, and Sweeney, Burbank with a Baedeker, A Cooking Egg, and The Hippopotamus follow, with whispers of immortality and Lune de Miel among them.

The poems are sharp, allusive, and often ironic, sketching a Europe of tourists, bankers, and weary talkers between the wars. Eliot's voice here is already distinct: cool, learned, and musical. The volume is a key early shelf for readers tracing the road to The Waste Land.
1568-poems:
William Ernest Henley's Poems, in the 1907 David Nutt edition, gather the verse of the poet best known for Invictus. A bust of Henley as frontispiece and a Shakespeare motto on love and summer flowers. The poems range from hospital sketches to London impressions and lyrics of courage under pain.

Henley, who knew suffering at first hand, writes with grit and music, and his short, strong lines carry a stoic temper. The tenth impression shows a book that found its readers. The volume is a good introduction to a Victorian poet of will, humour, and unflinching honesty.
1892-extracts-from-adam-s-diary-translat:
Mark Twain presents these extracts as Adam's diary, translated from the original manuscript. A note explains that he translated part of it years ago and has since deciphered more of Adam's hieroglyphs. Adam records Eden with a husband's bewilderment: Eve's questions, the animals, and the garden's rules.

A passage on tigers living on grass and flowers, when their teeth suggest they were meant to eat each other, shows Twain's method: Adam reasons solemnly. The reasoning itself is the joke. The diary is short, funny, and tender, and it pairs with Eve's diary as Twain's most affectionate retelling of Genesis.
1924-many-voices-poems:
E. Nesbit's Many Voices, poems published in 1922 and dedicated to her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-love Gertrude Bland, gathers lyrics written across her later years. The contents open with The Return, and the poems that follow move between love, war, and the English countryside.

A passage in which the comfortable are told they have taken the ease and the honor and left others the toil and the shame shows Nesbit's anger at wartime inequality. Other poems answer it with tenderness. Readers who know Nesbit only from The Railway Children will find a different writer here: a poet of strong feeling, plain speech, and a social conscience.
1962-a-defence-of-poesie-and-poems:
Sir Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesie, with his poems, is the founding work of English literary criticism. It was written in the 1580s to answer the charge that poetry is a waste of time. Sidney argues that the poet, unlike the historian or philosopher, does not merely describe what is, but creates what should be, and so teaches virtue more sweetly.

The poems that follow show Sidney practicing what he preaches: sonnets from Astrophil and Stella, songs, and lyrics of love and honor. The volume pairs argument with example, and it remains essential reading for anyone who wants to know how the Elizabethans thought about poetry, and why they thought it mattered.
20024-crankisms:
Lisle published Crankisms in 1901, a small book of short, sharp sayings about everyday life. One sample warns a reader not to call a favor a mere trifle. The person helped may take that claim at face value. Then the favor may never be repaid at all.

Each saying stands alone, so readers can dip in at any page. The tone is dry, wry, and a bit cranky, as the title promises. The book gives a quick taste of the brief moral wit that filled many small gift books of its time.
2008-mazelli-and-other-poems:
George W. Sands offers his first book of verse as a young American poet, hoping his country's literature might match its soldiers and statesmen. The title poem, Mazelli, leads a set of lyrics on love, nature, and national pride. Sands published the book in the 1840s, when American poets still looked to Britain for models and praise.

Sands writes in a plain, earnest voice, with an eye on Greece as the model of a people made great by letters. The poems are uneven, as first books often are, but they give a clear view of mid-nineteenth-century American ambition in verse. His preface speaks for a generation that wanted a national literature to match a growing republic.
20185-eventide-a-series-of-tales-and-poe:
Eventide gathers tales and poems for quiet evening reading, as its name suggests. The makers call their book a waif of weary moments at the start. They hope some warm-hearted spirit will shelter it from harsh critics. Will so small a booklet even draw a critic's arrows, they ask.

That modest plea sets a gentle tone for the pieces inside. Tales and verse alternate, suited to lampside calm at day's end. Victorian gift books often took this humble, hopeful pose with readers. Readers get soft sentiment and reflection in the classic evening mode.
20256-memoir-of-the-life-of-john-quincy-:
John Quincy Adams was born on July 11, 1767, in Braintree, Massachusetts. His parents were John and Abigail Adams, of Revolutionary fame. The town of his birth later became the town of Quincy. Their lives, the memoir notes, have already been ably illustrated elsewhere.

From that famed house, Adams rose to the highest posts in America. The memoir traces his schooling, travels, and long public service. It stresses character formed by stern parents and early hardship abroad. Readers get a compact life of a president raised inside the Revolution itself. His later years in Congress, fighting slavery's spread, crown his long career with honor.
20356-hero-and-leander-and-other-poems:
Hero and Leander is a famed love poem from Greek myth, told in English verse. A dedicatory letter offers the work to a patron's favorable allowance. The writer serves both himself and the deceased, he says humbly. He stands ready at his worship's disposing, now and ever.

Hero and Leander loved across the Hellespont, which he swam nightly. A storm and a drowned light end their tale in sorrow. Marlowe began the poem, and Chapman finished it after his death. Readers get one of the most beautiful English poems of the 1590s.
20373-the-dreamers-and-other-poems:
The Dreamers and Other Poems is a book of lyric verse by an unnamed poet. The poems turn on home, longing, and the pull of the open road. Short stanzas and plain images carry most of the feeling.

In one poem, a settled woman watches gypsies pass her door. She never guesses the wistful dream that draws them close. She never guesses the longing in each breast for a home like hers, where their hearts might rest. The book holds that tension throughout: the wish to wander set against the wish to stay.
20427-custer-and-other-poems:
Custer and Other Poems is a book of verse built around the memory of General Custer and the frontier West. Around the title poem stand reflective pieces on age, death, and the passing of fame. The poems use plain, ringing lines meant to be read aloud.

One poem warns those who burn the candle down to the stick. The sputtering socket, it says, yields but little light, and long life can be sadder than an early death. We must use, it urges, the warp and woof the ready present gives us. Such verses show the book's earnest, moral temper.
2044-the-education-of-henry-adams:
Henry Adams, grandson and great-grandson of presidents, writes his own education as a study of a man outpaced by his age. From Quincy and Harvard through Civil War diplomacy in London to Paris and Chicago, he tests each chapter of his life. Adams wrote the book in the third person, as if his own life were a case to study.

Adams judges himself a failure by the standards of the new century of dynamos, science, and mass power, and his irony cuts both ways. The memoir remains a classic of American self-scrutiny, praised for its style and its frank view of change. The famous Dynamo and Virgin chapter contrasts medieval faith with modern power, and readers still quote it.
20504-the-man-of-uz-and-other-poems:
The Man of Uz and Other Poems is a book of religious verse. The man of Uz is Job, the patient sufferer of the Old Testament. The title poem retells his story in measured lines, with his children and his losses before the reader.

The patriarch, with a chastened heart, joins his children's mirth. He keeps God's fear ever before him. Earnestly he brings his offerings and his prayers for every one of that beloved group, lest they have sinned in their feasting. The other poems share that devout temper, turning Bible scenes into verse for home reading.
20609-the-voyageur-and-other-poems:
William Henry Drummond's The Voyageur and Other Poems sings of French-Canadian river men, hunters, and habitant families. Drummond, a Montreal doctor, wrote in the dialect of his patients and friends. His recitation pieces were loved across Canada and the United States.

One poem opens on the night of the young New Year. The camp is warm and the fire is bright, and the bottle is close at hand. Out on the river the north wind blows, and down in the valley the snow lies piled. In that contrast — warm camp against deep winter — Drummond sets his tales of the old voyageur days.
20842-dreams:
Black fields, bright points that rise and sink, and spots of shifting colour open Dreams. Spots spread, shrink, and trade places in a slow, strange dance. Some dreamers see hues so bright, the text says, that waking sight cannot match them.

Thinkers of the mind stand behind studies of this kind. The book probes what dreams are and how they form. Sleep science was young, mixing keen notes with bold guesses about the night mind. Such books fed the new study of sleep. It treats the night mind as a thing to be studied, not feared.
20914-a-window-in-thrums:
A bare house, a manse, and Hendry's cot watch the brae in A Window in Thrums. J. M. Barrie sets his 1896 tale in a poor row of homes in a Scots village. A broken dyke alone keeps the potato pit from the south road.

Thrums, Barrie's famed fictional Kirriemuir, fills the tales seen from one window. Weavers, elders, joys, and griefs pass in warm, wry sketches. Barrie wrote of his mother's world with love and sly humour. Before Peter Pan, books like this made his name, and they still show his tender art at its roots.
21029-the-new-morning-poems:
A silent flame of pure passion before the true and good marks one life in Alfred Noyes's poems. The New Morning, from 1918, praises a man who scorned to fawn on the crowd. All might see what he saw, the verse says, who truly would.

Noyes, famed for The Highwayman, gathers war-age poems of hope and grief here. A new morning after darkness gives the book its title and its trust. Music drives his lines, ballad-sure and bright even in sorrow. Readers who love classic, singing verse will find Noyes's gift intact across these pages of loss and dawn.
21419-the-children-some-educational-prob:
Alexander Darroch, professor of education at Edinburgh, takes up schooling in The Children, issued in 1907. He finds the system of his day full of faults, with no clear join between its parts. Each part, he says, chases its own aims with little link to the rest.

Chapters treat the state's role in schooling, its cost, and its care for health. Darroch covers medical checks of children, the feeding of poor pupils, and physical training. He also asks what education is for, and how its means should be ordered. The book is a clear survey of reform debates in Edwardian Britain.
21872-the-life-of-david-as-reflected-in-:
David's life is read through his own songs in Alexander Maclaren's study. The Life of David as Reflected in His Psalms reached its ninth edition in 1903. Maclaren, a famed preacher, calls David's life remarkable for its romantic variety of circumstance. Shepherd boy, exile, king, and penitent each gather fresh fitness, he says, for David's great work: giving voice to every phase of devout feeling.

Chapters follow the early days, the long exile in its stages, the kingship, and the tears of the penitent. A final chapter studies the songs of the fugitive. The book belongs to the Household Library of Exposition, made for Bible classes and home study. It treats the Psalms as a diary of the soul, keyed to the events of David's life.
21921-pickwickian-manners-and-customs:
Dickens's Pickwick Papers had grown a literature of its own by 1897, and Percy Fitzgerald catalogs it in Pickwickian Manners and Customs. No English book, he says, so increased the general gaiety of the country. Sixty years on, readers still devoured Pickwick, counted its misprints, and prized the earliest states of its plates. Fitzgerald inscribes his study to Augustine Birrell, himself a noted Dickens lover.

The book walks through the customs, places, and people of the novel's world. Rochester and Dickens Land, then as now, drew pilgrims to the scenes. Fitzgerald treats a comic novel like a classic under glass, with a fan's joy and a scholar's patience. For Pickwick lovers, it is a companion full of garnish for a favorite dish.
22052-standish-of-standish-a-story-of-th:
Jane G. Austin wrote Standish of Standish, a story of the Pilgrims, in 1889. Austin came of old New England stock and spent years on Plymouth records. She opens by noting how Americans pause to look back at the spot where the Pilgrims sowed their seed. Her tale gives that looking-back a human form in Myles Standish, the colony's soldier captain.

Around Standish she builds the daily life of early Plymouth. Hunger, Indians, weddings, and quarrels fill the small settlement's first years. Austin fills gaps in the record with invention, and says so honestly. Her Pilgrim novels helped fix the popular picture of Plymouth for generations of readers.
22301-valley-of-dreams:
Valley of Dreams is a work of fiction preserved from Project Gutenberg, with no author or date in the catalog record. The surviving scene is a fast, slangy talk about pictures of the moon. The speakers hope those shots will pack crowds to the doors.

They also count on broadcast rights to pull their trip out of the red. A profit, they joke, might even come through for the Academy. That mix of space travel, film, and money gives the tale its flavor. It reads as early popular science fiction, built around a showy voyage and the businessmen hoping to cash in on it.
22322-a-legend-of-old-persia-and-other-p:
A Legend of Old Persia and Other Poems collects verse built on an old eastern tale. No poet is named in the catalog record. The legend opens in a golden climate, in the fairest place on earth.

Its happy people suffer no sickness, plague, or want. They live through endless summers, and half-summers hardly colder. Growing older so slowly, they hardly guess the years are passing. That dreamlike start sets the tone for the title poem. The other poems share the volume with it. Readers get romantic verse of a kind once read aloud: smooth, storied, and set far from daily life.
22423-poems:
Poems, preserved without an author's name in the record, opens on a cold landscape. The dim sea glints chill under a shy white sun. Skeleton weeds stand white with frost by a hilltop finger-post.

Rough, long grasses by the post never dry out. Traveller's-joy smoke puffs over hawthorn berry and hazel tuft. Such images give the verse a wintry, rural English cast. The poems favor observed nature over grand statement or story. Small signs of season and road carry the feeling here. Readers who like quiet landscape poetry will find its mood familiar. It rewards attention to frost, weed, and berry alike.
22569-the-listeners-and-other-poems:
Walter de la Mare wrote The Listeners and Other Poems, a landmark verse collection. De la Mare's title poem is among the most famous short poems in English. Its traveller knocks at a moonlit door and finds only listeners.

Other poems in the volume share his quiet, haunted music. One tells of blossoms coming to berries on slender stalks. A lady is charmed away for one long summer's day. Vows sweet, merry, and tender accompany that charmed summer absence. De la Mare mixes childlike wonder with an undertow of mystery. His lyrics seem simple until their strangeness settles on the reader. The collection remains a doorway into modern English poetry's dream side.
22650-the-defence-of-guenevere-and-other:
The Defence of Guenevere and Other Poems is William Morris's first book of verse, a landmark of Pre-Raphaelite poetry. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Morris retells Arthurian tales in a voice by turns dreamy and stark, quite unlike the polished verse around him.

In the sample, a knight knows somehow that he is Launcelot, bravest of all who ever bore lance or swung sword in wrong cause or right. Guenevere's defense at her trial gives the title poem its dramatic frame: the queen pleading her life before Arthur's court. Other poems treat Froissart's chronicles and northern legend. The book still startles with its color, violence, and medieval longing.
22717-lundy-s-lane-and-other-poems:
Lundy's Lane and Other Poems, published by the George H. Doran Company in 1916, gathers verse by the Canadian poet Duncan Campbell Scott. The catalog record credits the publisher. The title poem recalls the battle of Lundy's Lane, the bloodiest fight of the War of 1812, fought near Niagara Falls in July 1814.

The sample comes from a love lyric: in her twilight garden she plucked a half-opened rose, and the speaker thought it meant for him. She hid it in her bosom instead, and the unanswered question of her meaning haunts him still. Scott mixes such lyrics with sonnets and war-haunted meditations. The volume shows Canada's leading poet of the day at his most musical and melancholy.
22732-last-poems:
Edward Thomas wrote the poems collected in Last Poems, the final gathering of a poet killed at Arras in 1917. The catalog record gives no year. Thomas came late to verse, writing all his poems in the last years of his life, most of them rooted in the English countryside he walked and loved.

In the sample lines, the poet wishes for the speech of trees and birds, a language that cannot be betrayed. What was hid should still be hid, except from those made like him, who answer when such whispers bid. That quiet creed runs through the volume: rain, roads, old houses, and the approach of war. Thomas's restraint made him a founder of modern English nature poetry, and these last poems carry his voice at its purest.
22734-bay-a-book-of-poems:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Bay, a small book of poems shaped by the First World War. The catalog record's credit line is garbled, and no year is given. Lawrence, then known for Sons and Lovers, gathered in Bay the war poems he had written through the conflict's years, fierce and grieving by turns.

The sample shows his manner: a general canters gaily past, his white plumes winking under a grey evening sky. Then the earth itself seems to stir. A red ridge heaves up in slow, magnetic answer. Landscape and artillery merge in a single ominous image. Lawrence's war verse is less famous than his novels, but it burns with the same intensity. Bay is a slim, strange book from a major writer at war's end.
22736-the-inn-of-dreams:
The Inn of Dreams is a book of lyric poems, dreamy and musical in the manner of the 1890s. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its title promises lodging for the night thoughts: an inn where fairy princes ride and beauty keeps her brief hour.

The sample calls to those princes: in the night you have been dreamed of, O fairy Princes, and her eyes shine bright. Spur your swift horses: this is Beauty's hour. Beauty's flame, the poem says, quivers and flickers out like a golden flame in a dark place, a torch and wonder of the world. Such verse prizes shimmer over statement. The collection will suit readers who like their poetry perfumed, twilit, and unashamedly romantic.
22739-the-human-aura-astral-colors-and-t:
Swami Panchadasi wrote The Human Aura: Astral Colors and Thought Forms, a handbook of occult teaching about the colored atmosphere said to surround every person. The catalog record gives no year. Panchadasi, one of the pen names of the New Thought writer William Walker Atkinson, taught thousands of mail-order students in the era's hidden wisdom.

The contents promise a key to the astral colors. Red stands for the physical, blue for the spiritual, yellow for the mental. White and black stand as the two poles of spirituality, and olive, russet, and citrine arise from mixing. With practice, the book claims, almost everyone can learn to see the prana aura's outlines plainly. It is a period document of popular occultism, written with a teacher's confidence in invisible things.
22803-helen-redeemed-and-other-poems:
Maurice Hewlett wrote Helen Redeemed and Other Poems, a volume of narrative verse by the novelist of The Forest Lovers. The catalog record gives no year. Hewlett, a romantic medievalist in prose, here takes up classical story: Helen of Troy, redeemed at last from the blame the poets laid on her.

The sample sings of Odysseus and his long road home. What weariness of wind, wave, and foam lay before him first! Only then would he see his home of scrub and crag again. What stress of pilgrimage awaited him, through roaring waterways and the cities of men. What sojourns among folk beyond mortal seafarers' ken. Hewlett's verse rolls in long, sonorous lines, more incantation than argument. The volume shows the late-romantic taste for myth retold in music, by a writer who believed the old tales still carried fire.
2355-the-formation-of-vegetable-mould-th:
Charles Darwin's last book argues that earthworms, tiny and ignored, have shaped the landscape itself. The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms shows how worms bury stones, build soil, and slowly remake fields, with Darwin's experiments measuring their work over years. The book is a model of patient observation.

Darwin's final argument is humble and grand at once: small causes, given time, move the world. The work charmed general readers and remains a classic of natural history. Anyone curious about Darwin beyond evolution will find a delightful surprise.
2491-love-or-fame-and-other-poems:
Fannie Isabelle Sherrick's Love or Fame, and Other Poems offers Victorian lyrics on love, ambition, and the choices women faced between domestic life and public praise. The poems are musical, sentimental, and earnest, with the title poem framing the volume's central question. Sherrick writes in the popular style of her day.

The collection interests readers of women's poetry and period verse, even where the poems feel conventional now. Its sincerity carries many pieces. Poetry lovers will find a representative voice of its age. Sherrick published her poems in magazines before gathering them here.
2558-poems:
George P. Morris, the American songwriter and editor, gathered his verse in this volume, from his early days in New York letters. Morris wrote songs and ballads that ordinary readers sang and quoted, and his lines favor clear feeling over showy craft.

The poems run from patriotic airs to home and nature lyrics, with the plain music that made his name. Readers will find the popular taste of early America here, warm, sentimental, and direct. The book serves as a record of a poet who reached his public through melody as much as print.
263-trees-and-other-poems:
Joyce Kilmer's 1914 volume holds the poem that made him famous and many quieter ones. Trees and Other Poems opens with a dedication to his mother, gentlest of critics, and a Patmore epigraph on humble rhyme. Schoolboy verse, praised by that mother, gives way to mature lyrics.

Trees itself praises a tree's beauty in simple quatrains, ending with the claim that poems are made by fools like me. Other poems treat faith, home, and nature with the same plain music. Kilmer, killed in France in 1918, left this book as his best-known work. It remains a favorite gift volume.
264-main-street-and-other-poems:
Joyce Kilmer, best known for Trees, gathers here poems of streets, houses, and faith. Main Street and Other Poems, transcribed from the 1917 edition, opens with its title poem for S. M. L. and moves through roofs, snowmen, and valentines. Many pieces first ran in periodicals.

Later poems honor Lionel Johnson, Father Gerard Hopkins, and Rupert Brooke, and visit Rheims Cathedral and wartime seas. Kilmer's verse is plain, musical, and devout, with a love of home and church. The book shows the poet killed in 1918 at his most varied. It pairs well with his Trees volume.
2888-yorkshire-dialect-poems-1673-1915-a:
F. W. Moorman, professor of English language at Leeds, compiled Yorkshire Dialect Poems from 1673 to 1915 with traditional poems and a historical introduction. Published for the Yorkshire Dialect Society in 1916 and 1917, the book is dedicated to Yorkshiremen serving in trench or on battleship. Contents include a dialogue between an old wife, a lass, and a butcher, Henry Carey's Honest Yorkshireman, and verses from Snaith Marsh.

The poems speak in dialect throughout, with glosses for words such as kine for cattle and pail for a milking vessel. One song follows a lad who runs away to London with ribbed stockings, waistcoats, money, and a light heart. The collection preserves a regional voice across two and a half centuries, useful to readers of dialect verse and local history.
3039-forty-two-poems:
James Elroy Flecker collected Forty-Two Poems as a slim volume of lyrics, sonnets, and exotic fantasies. The poems move between London streets and imagined lands. Evening falls on smoky walls, railings drip with rain, and a tram glides solemnly like love's still-mysterious car, lit gold and white with a single dark red star. A garden beyond the Thames holds a rose where flowers are pale and few. The first sonnet of Bathrolaire opens over a moonless land, showing Flecker's taste for invented kingdoms and musical names.

His verse favors color, mystery, and a young man's longing. The collection suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century lyric poetry before Flecker's early death cut his promise short.
312-young-adventure-a-book-of-poems:
Stephen Vincent Benét, aged twenty, dedicates his first book to a friend who was Perseus, D'Artagnan, and Lancelot to him. Young Adventure, from the 1918 American edition, gathers poems first printed in periodicals. Titles were conformed for ease of searching.

Benét's early verse mixes romance, war, and youthful ambition in musical lines. The book predates his Pulitzer work by years, yet shows his gift for story in verse. Readers meet a poet learning his craft in public. The volume charms as a debut of real promise. Benét later won Pulitzers for poetry and for John Brown's Body.
317-the-culprit-fay-and-other-poems:
Joseph Rodman Drake's fairy poem opens with purged eyes seeing old fairyland's tinsel show. The Culprit Fay and Other Poems, from the 1836 Dearborn edition, was inscribed by the author's daughter to Fitz-Greene Halleck. Drake died young, and friends gathered his verse.

The index lists To a Friend, Leon, Niagara, and The American Flag among the shorter pieces. The Culprit Fay itself tells of a fairy punished for loving a mortal. Drake's Hudson River scenery and romantic fancy charmed early American readers. The volume preserves a brief, bright career. Drake's fairy verse still charms readers of early American poetry.
3525-music-and-other-poems:
Henry van Dyke gathers poems in this volume, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in October 1904. The contents divide into odes, sonnets, legends, and lyrics. Odes include Music, Peace, and God of the Open Air, while sonnets treat work, life, love, and the child in the garden. Legends such as A Legend of Service and The Vain King sit beside shorter lyrics.

Van Dyke writes in a warm, musical style, often turning to nature, faith, and the duties of a good life. His poems favor clear images and steady rhythms over experiment. The collection suits readers who enjoy traditional verse for reading aloud, with themes of service, home, and the seasons running through it.
353-in-flanders-fields-and-other-poems:
War poems by Canadian doctor and soldier John McCrae anchor this small volume, drawn from the 1919 New York text. Most pieces date from 1894 to 1917, and a short essay on McCrae by his friend Andrew Macphail opens the book. The verse moves from love, sleep, and old towns to the strain of war.

The title poem speaks in the voice of dead soldiers in Flanders, urging the living to keep faith with them. Other poems mourn fallen men, praise duty, and mark places such as Quebec and Isandlwana. Read as a whole, the book shows a poet shaped first by peace, then by loss on the front.
3530-love-at-arms:
Rafael Sabatini sets this romance in Renaissance Italy, opening with a dedication to Guidobaldo da Montefeltro and an epigraph from Ariosto on ladies, knights, arms, and loves. Chapters carry titles such as Vox Populi, On a Mountain Path, Sackcloth and Motley, Monna Valentina, and The Amorous Duke. The hero moves through courts, wine shops, and mountain roads in a world of dukes and intriguers.

Love and swordplay drive the plot, with a fool's motley and a duke's desire both shaping events. Sabatini writes with speed and color, giving his hero duels, disguises, and a love that must survive politics. Readers who enjoy historical romance in the manner of his Captain Blood books will find a brisk, old fashioned adventure here.
3665-maurine-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers her long poem Maurine with other poems in this popular edition of 1910. Maurine itself, a narrative poem of love and fate, fills the first hundred pages. Shorter pieces follow, such as All Roads that Lead to God are Good, Dust Sealed, Advice, Over the Banisters, The Past, Secrets, Applause, and The Story. Wilcox adds many new poems to this edition.

Wilcox writes in clear, musical verse about love, faith, and the choices of women. Her speakers move from morning mail and a lover's scorn to thoughts of God and the past. The book suits readers who enjoy popular American poetry of the late nineteenth century, earnest, romantic, and meant to be shared.
400-helen-of-troy-and-other-poems:
Sara Teasdale gathers early lyrics in this 1911 volume, opening with a sequence on Helen of Troy. Poems on Beatrice, Sappho, Guenevere, and Erinna follow, each giving a famed woman a brief, clear voice. Later pieces turn to love songs, city scenes, and quiet laments in New York parks and streets.

Teasdale writes in short, musical lines, with plain words and sharp feeling. Love, loss, and beauty recur, never dressed in heavy show. The book marks her early gift: to say much in few lines, and to let a single image carry a whole mood.
4009-the-victories-of-love-and-other-poe:
Coventry Patmore's poems trace love through marriage, doubt, and faith, with Leah and Rachel as figures for two kinds of devotion. The speaker weighs the weary work of forcing love on one who has enough of it, and the honor owed to a woman whose thoughts stand too high for flattery.

Other poems in the volume carry the same theme in shorter forms, joining domestic life to spiritual hope. Patmore writes in measured, earnest verse, closer to prayer than to show. Readers who enjoy Victorian religious poetry will find a serious, tender book about love that seeks to serve rather than to win.
424-general-william-booth-enters-into-he:
Vachel Lindsay gathers poems of faith, reform, and American life in this 1913 volume, reprinted in 1916. The title poem marches Salvation Army founder William Booth into heaven to drums, banjos, and a host of saved sinners. Other pieces praise Lincoln, Shakespeare, and St. Francis, and scold drunkards, gamblers, and unrepentant cities.

Lindsay writes in chanting, musical lines meant to be read aloud, with strong beats and plain speech. Springfield, cornfields, and street corners ground his visions. The book marks Lindsay as a people's poet, eager to preach beauty and justice in the same breath.
4331-sun-up-and-other-poems:
Lola Ridge wrote this collection of poems after her Ghetto book, and she dedicated it to her mother. The opening dedication cradles the speaker back into darkness, half shapes, and the dust of unused air. It sets a tone of memory, loss, and stubborn tenderness that runs through the book.

The contents divide into Sun-Up, Monologues, Windows, and Secrets, with poems on jaguars, wild ducks, trains, skyscrapers, and Wall Street at night. Ridge moves between nature and the city, between a train window and an inner room. Her free verse keeps the immigrant city and the American landscape in the same frame.
4332-the-ghetto-and-other-poems:
Lola Ridge wrote the title poem of this collection for the American people, offering a harsh feast, with iron still hot from the furnace. The Ghetto pictures the crowded Jewish quarter of New York, with its markets, faces, fog, and debris, in free verse of great force.

Other poems range across Manhattan, Broadway, the Bowery, and Brooklyn Bridge, with pieces on iron, labor, and the war years. Frank Little at Calvary and The Song of Iron show Ridge's political edge. The book stands as an early modernist portrait of immigrant New York, written from inside its streets.
5015-state-of-the-union-addresses-of-joh:
John Quincy Adams's State of the Union addresses open with thanks for providence. Health prevails within American borders. Abundance covers the land despite the seasons. Peace holds with all nations, and calm holds at home. The sixth president frames his messages as reports on a republic blessed and obliged to use its blessings well.

Internal improvements, commerce, and the nation's standing abroad fill the later messages, delivered in Adams's learned and moralizing style. The set covers a presidency that prized science, roads, and canals over party combat. Readers get a primary record of the 1820s, when America debated what a national government should build.
5134-discoveries-made-upon-men-and-matte:
Ben Jonson's Discoveries gathers the short notes, judgments, and reflections he made from his daily reading, arranged as a wood, or storehouse, of thoughts on men, letters, and conduct. The volume pairs those prose fragments with poems, including his famous memorial lines to William Shakespeare and an epitaph for the boy actor Salathiel Pavy.

Jonson writes with a scholar's eye and a playwright's bluntness, praising, correcting, and moralising in turn. Readers get a direct look at how a leading Jacobean writer thought about his craft and his contemporaries, in pieces short enough to dip into and sharp enough to quote.
5209-miscellaneous-poems:
This collection of miscellaneous poems opens with Sir Eustace Grey, a dramatic poem set in a madhouse, where a visitor, a physician, and a patient speak in turn. The ruined lord of Greyling Hall, once admired by rich and poor alike, tells how pride and rash deeds brought him to his cell. The physician urges the visitor on to happier scenes.

The remaining contents, The Hall of Justice, Woman, The Birth of Flattery, and Reflections, extend the volume's moral range. Readers will find verse that mixes dramatic monologue with satire and reflection, in the style of early nineteenth-century narrative poetry at its most earnest.
544-anne-s-house-of-dreams:
Lucy Maud Montgomery follows Anne Shirley into married life at Four Winds in this Anne novel. Done with teaching geometry, Anne leaves Green Gables garret for a small house of dreams with Gilbert Blythe. Captain Jim, Miss Cornelia, and Leslie Moore, a girl in a sad marriage, fill the harbor town.

Montgomery writes with warmth and wit, mixing joy, loss, and gossip. A first child, a life book, and a ship of dreams mark Anne's new life. The book endures as a tender chapter of Anne's growth, where a young wife learns that dreams hold both light and shadow.
5616-the-madman-his-parables-and-poems:
Kahlil Gibran wrote The Madman as a book of parables and poems, opening with the story of how he became a madman. One day, long before many gods were born, he woke from deep sleep to find all seven masks he had fashioned and worn in seven lives stolen. Running maskless through crowded streets shouting thieves, he was laughed at, feared, and finally named madman by a youth on a housetop.

When he looked up, the sun kissed his naked face for the first time, and he felt freed rather than shamed. The parables that follow speak in that freed voice, about gods, men, love, and sorrow. Readers get Gibran's early masterpiece in miniature: short, lyrical pieces that read like proverbs.
592-the-chinese-nightingale-and-other-po:
Vachel Lindsay gathers chanting poems of America at war and at peace in this volume, dedicated to Sara Teasdale. The title poem, which won the Levinson Prize in Poetry magazine for 1915, tells of a Chinese nightingale in musical, painted lines. Later sections watch the war from August 1914 to April 1917, then America at war.

Lindsay writes in strong, singing rhythms meant for voice, with prairie, flag, and factory in his sights. Poems on Bryan, Jane Addams, Mark Twain, and Joan of Arc mix politics with fancy. The book shows Lindsay as a people's poet, eager to sing a nation through hard years.
5953-many-kingdoms:
Elizabeth Jordan's Many Kingdoms opens with children, imagination, and a kingdom of the mind, under an epigraph comparing the state of man to a little kingdom suffering nature's insurrections. Margaret Hamilton Perry listens remotely as Raymond Mortimer explains that a little girl comes to play, seen by no one but him, and Margaret answers candidly that pretending seems little fun. With delicacy, she adds that she will like the girl and play with her if Raymond does.

The story follows a novel of inner kingdoms, where childhood fancy, adult feeling, and social life contend for rule. Jordan, author of May Iverson and Tales of the Cloister, writes with sympathy for imagined companions and real loneliness. The book suits readers who enjoy novels of childhood imagination grown serious, and stories where a private kingdom shapes a public life.
6025-the-englishman-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathers poems headed by The Queen's Last Ride, written on the day of Queen Victoria's funeral. The Queen takes a drive with the carriage way hung in purple, army and navy leading, kings and princes riding behind as a humble band, and flags of all nations at half-mast.

The silent lady of royal birth rides away from earth's courts and unrest toward a mystical goal on a secret quest. Wilcox writes in plain, musical verse, fond of direct feeling and large occasions. The collection moves from royal mourning to other English themes, with sentiment worn openly.
6061-some-poems:
This small volume adds a few poems by Sir Walter Scott to a larger collection, since room remained for more verses. The introduction notes the first was written in 1811 during the struggle with Napoleon in the Peninsula, and the second in 1815, after Waterloo.

The contents list The Vision of Don Roderick, The Field of Waterloo, The Dance of Death, Romance of Dunois, The Troubadour, and Pibroch of Donald Dhu. Over all hangs a thin haze of battle, through which only finer feelings and nobler hopes show. Scott's war poems look toward a day when war shall be no more.
6062-pike-county-ballads-and-other-poems:
John Hay's Pike County Ballads lead this collection, with Jim Bludso, Little Breeches, Banty Tim, the Mystery of Gilgal, and the Pledge at Spunky Point. An introduction by Henry Morley frames the poems, which mix western humor with river and prairie voices.

Wanderlieder follow, from sunrise in the Place de la Concorde and the Sphinx of the Tuileries to the curse of Hungary and the monks of Basle. Later pieces include Miles Keogh's Horse, the Advance-Guard, a haunted room, and songs of liberty, remorse, and homecoming. Hay writes with vigor and plain feeling.
6121-jack-winters-gridiron-chums:
Mark Overton opens Jack Winters' Gridiron Chums with grueling football practice. A shrill whistle halts almost two dozen sturdy boys in their middle teens, clad in old and new football togs and struggling furiously. The coach, acting as referee in practice, stops the commotion as if by magic.

Chapters follow a boy in trouble, Big Bob confessing, a friend in need, a message from Marshall, and Jack and Joel investigating. The great game opens, struggle fills the gridiron, and glory follows, before bed fire burns in Chester and a burning house tests the chums. Overton praises team play on and off the field.
617-poems:
Alan Seeger gathers his short life's verse in this volume, with an introduction by William Archer. Juvenilia, sonnets, Paris poems, and translations from Dante and Ariosto fill the early pages. Last poems from the Aisne and Champagne in 1914-15 close the book, including I Have a Rendezvous with Death.

Seeger, an American poet killed in France on 4 July 1916, writes in polished, romantic lines, full of beauty, youth, and fate. His war poems face death with grave acceptance, not swagger. The volume endures as a poignant record of a young poet who kept his rendezvous.
6332-playful-poems:
Henry Morley edits this volume of Companion Poets, with an introduction, gathering playful poems from Chaucer to Hood. Chaucer's Manciple's tale of Phoebus and the crow, modernised by Leigh Hunt, opens, with Sir Thopas, the Friar's tale of summoner and devil, and the Reeve's tale. Wordsworth modernises the Cuckoo and the Nightingale, Gower gives treasure trove, and Lydgate, Dunbar, and Drayton follow.

Pope's Rape of the Lock, Cowper's John Gilpin, and Burns's Tam o'Shanter carry the fun forward. Hood's demon ship and tale of a trumpet follow, with a note on ombre and a glossary to close. Morley, emeritus professor at University College London, presents old humour in modern dress, so that readers can enjoy it without a scholar's apparatus. The 1891 book is light verse with a learned frame.
651-phantasmagoria-and-other-poems:
Lewis Carroll gathers his comic and serious verse in this volume, first published in 1869 and reprinted by Macmillan in 1911 with illustrations by Arthur B. Frost. Phantasmagoria, in seven cantos, tells of a man who finds a ghost in his study one winter night, cold, tired, and cross, and learns the ghost's five rules. Echoes, A Sea Dirge, Hiawatha's Photographing, and The Three Voices follow.

Carroll writes with logic games, parody, and sudden tenderness, dedicating the book to a dear child and golden summer hours. The poems show the Alice author's other side: a wit who could rhyme a ghost into manners. The volume charms as a varied Carroll set, where nonsense and feeling sit side by side.
6568-sociology-and-modern-social-problem:
Charles A. Ellwood, a professor at the University of Missouri, wrote this short text for classes that had little time for sociology. The first eight chapters lay out its basic ideas through the family, seen as a typical human group, with its growth, shape, and work. Later chapters turn those ideas on live problems of his day, side by side with lessons from economics.

Ellwood teaches by cases, not by dry rules, and aims at readers in extension courses and teachers' reading circles as much as at college students. The book is plain, orderly, and meant to be used, not just read. It offers a clear, early view of how a new science tried to make sense of modern social life.
6623-the-coming-of-the-princess-and-othe:
Kate Seymour MacLean of Kingston, Ontario, gathers her poems in a volume introduced by G. Mercer Adam, editor of The Canadian Monthly. Adam, who had often printed her verse, acts as foster father to the book, and bespeaks a kind welcome from Canadian readers. He calls her a child of the first winds and suns of a young nation.

The title poem on a princess's coming leads a set of lyrics on home, land, and feeling, in the clear style of her day. MacLean writes with a Canadian eye and a gentle hand. The Coming of the Princess is a pleasant, early Canadian poetry book, worth a look for lovers of Dominion verse.
679-poems:
Frances E. W. Harper gathered her verse in this 1895 volume, with poems on home, faith, and public life. Titles such as "My Mother's Kiss", "The Dying Bondman", and "An Appeal to My Country Women" show the range: tender family scenes sit beside direct calls for justice. Her voice is plain and musical, meant to be read aloud and felt at once.

Many poems speak from the experience of Black Americans after slavery, praising courage, mourning loss, and urging moral action. Others turn to nature, childhood, and prayer. The book stands as a key record of a leading Black woman poet of the age, joining lyric craft to a public conscience in short, clear verse.
6815-old-spookses-pass-malcolm-s-katie-a:
Isabella Valancy Crawford, dedicating her poems to her uncle John Irwin Crawford, opens Old Spookses' Pass with a camp on Yaller Bull Flat. Possum Billy, Tom, and the speaker, all smart at throwing a lariat and riding a bronco, argue square with a devil rolled in a mule's hide. The verse speaks in a rough, western voice, full of sinew and humor.

Malcolm's Katie and other poems follow, with Canadian scenes, loves, and frontier talk. Crawford writes with a pioneer's vigor and a poet's ear. Old Spookses' Pass is a lively, distinctive book of Canadian verse, rough-edged and full of life.
6859-songs-of-labor-and-other-poems:
Morris Rosenfeld, translated from Yiddish by Rose Pastor Stokes and Helena Frank, sings songs of labor in a factory where machines roar so wildly that workers can scarce hear themselves think. Contents run from In the Factory and My Boy to The Nightingale to the Workman, Despair, Whither, and From Dawn to Dawn. A candle seller, a pale operator, and a beggar family join the chorus.

Rosenfeld writes as a sweatshop poet, with anger, pity, and hope in plain, musical verse. His songs gave voice to immigrant workers. Songs of Labor is a moving, historic book of Yiddish labor poetry in English dress.
6957-canada-and-other-poems:
T F Young offers these poems with great diffidence, yet with a purpose that steadies him: to do something for his country, as Burns did for his. Canadian literature, he warns in his preface, stands in its infancy, and it must not stay so if the nation is to grow great. Literature, he writes, gives life to a nation, or mirrors its life and thought in a glass that cheers, strengthens, and ennobles.

The poems that follow sing of Canada and other themes, aiming to help a young literature grow with its people. Young asks readers to judge the verses by their intent as much as their polish. The book stands as an early Canadian bid for a national voice in verse, modest in claim and earnest in hope.
7034-fleurs-de-lys-and-other-poems:
Arthur Weir gathers Fleurs de Lys and other poems, dedicating the volume lovingly to his parents William and Elizabeth Somerville Weir, his most severe and kindly critics. An epigraph holds that only he is a poet who finds happiness in sorrow, light in darkness, and love everywhere, leading fellow kind by flowery paths toward life's sunny height. Weir chose the name Fleurs de Lys for the Canadian poems opening the book.

Their scenes belong to the monarchial, or Fleur de Lys, period of France in Canada, whose royal crest graced the cover. Many poems first appeared in the Montreal and Toronto press, and their kindly reception led the author to collect them. The volume sings Canada's French past and its present in verse.
7110-rose-and-roof-tree-poems:
George Parsons Lathrop gathers Rose and Roof Tree poems, opening with an illustration of Jessamine and verses on the enchanted ladder of rhyme, climbed round by round and patiently. A dedication says the verse needs no hint of whom it sings for, since the rose, knowing her own right, makes light rays her servants to carry her color. Every line, the poet promises, breathes of her whom it seeks, however unworthily, to serve and honor.

Contents list Windfalls, Rose and Roof Tree, Music of Growth, A Song Long Ago, and Melancholy Contentment, then an April aria, the bobolink, the sun shower, and June longings. A rune of rain, the song sparrow, Fairhaven Bay, and a chant for autumn follow, with moods of love in absence and heart's fountain. Lathrop sings nature and love in measured verse.
7130-london-films:
W D Howells sketches London Films in twenty chapters, from meteorological emotions and civic and social comparisons, mostly odious, to shows and side shows of state. The dun year's brilliant flower, the sights and sounds of streets, and misgivings as to the American invasion follow. A seat in the gallery of the Commons and the means of sojourn come next. Certain traits of the London springtime and voluntary and involuntary sightseeing lead to glimpses of the lowly and the lowlier.

Twice seen sights and half fancied facts, an afternoon at Hampton Court, and a Sunday morning in the country precede fishing for whitebait and Henley Day. American origins, mostly northern and mostly southern, close the set with aspects, intimations, and parting guests. Illustrations show Parliament, Fleet Street, Hyde Park, and Rotten Row.
7228-laura-secord-the-heroine-of-1812-a-:
Sarah Anne Curzon wrote the drama Laura Secord to rescue a brave woman's name from oblivion and set it in its proper place among Canadian heroes. She dedicates the volume to all true Canadians, of whatever derivation, and pairs the play with other poems. The epigraphs invoke white-robed bards telling tales of old and the search for what is beautiful, true, and noble in a book.

Secord's walk through danger in 1812 becomes a stage story of courage, told in verse drama rather than in prose history. Curzon's preface frames the play as an act of national memory, claiming a heroine for a young country. The poems that follow widen the book from one deed to a fuller Canadian voice.
7325-dreams-and-days-poems:
George Parsons Lathrop's Dreams and Days gathers poems in four parts, opening with a call to young men, a star, sunshine, jessamine, the bobolink, and a sailor's song returning. Bride brook, May-rose, the singing wire, the heart of a song, and south-wind follow, with a lover's year, new worlds, night in New York, and the song-sparrow widening the book's range.

Later poems turn to war's bride, a rune of rain, breakers, a child-year, christening, and thanksgiving. Then come youth, the sword, the golden gate, charity, Helen at the loom, and a casket of opals. Lathrop dedicates the book to Rosl, and his verse mixes domestic feeling with public occasion. The collection shows a minor American poet at his most musical.
7336-home-lyrics-a-book-of-poems:
H. S. Battersby's Home Lyrics, volume two, appeared after the author's death, published by her children in fulfilment of her last wishes. It is dedicated to the memory of the dearest of mothers, whose whole life was consecrated to their happiness. Her children write that she fully reciprocated their self-denial, devotion, and love, and the book stands as a family memorial in verse.

Its index runs from a son who passed from earth in April 1887 through birdies, a little five-year-old, and the angel on war. A rink, a Binghampton home, and Mrs Langtry as Miss Hardcastle in She Stoops to Conquer follow. Domestic affection, loss, and home scenes fill the lyrics. The volume preserves a mother's voice, kept by those who loved her.
772-moral-emblems:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote and illustrated these short poems, first printed at the Davos Press by his stepson Lloyd Osbourne. Each poem pairs with a woodcut, and the emblems turn on labour, cross, and crown, on duty, death, and hope. A preface by Osbourne sets the small book in its place.

The verses are brief, earnest, and a touch quaint, the work of a sick man writing for friends. Their charm lies in the mix of word and image, and in Stevenson's moral seriousness beneath the play. The book is a curiosity for Stevenson lovers, showing the poet at his most private and devout.
795-ballads-and-lyrics-of-old-france-wit:
Andrew Lang translated ballads and lyrics of old France in this 1872 volume, with other poems of his own. Charles d'Orléans opens the set with spring songs and rondels, and François Villon and other medieval poets follow. Lang renders their grace and melancholy into English verse that keeps the old music.

The book introduced many English readers to French medieval lyric, from courtly love to thieves' slang. Lang's versions are light, faithful, and musical, and his notes name each poet in turn. The volume stands as a charming bridge between France and Britain, and as a model of how translation can keep a distant age alive.
856-dreams:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short comic piece on dreams, opening with the strangest he ever had. Going into a theatre, he fancies the cloak-room attendant stops him and insists he leave his legs behind. He is not surprised, he notes, for his knowledge of theatre folk would bar surprise at any demand, even in a dream.

Jerome spins the fancy into a meditation on how dreams mix sense and nonsense, fear and farce. His tone is light, wry, and confessional, the idle fellow at his best. The piece is brief, but it shows Jerome's gift for turning a small absurdity into a pleasant essay on the mind at play.
980-alice-adams:
Booth Tarkington wrote this novel about Alice Adams, a young woman of a middling family in an American town, who longs for a place in society. Her father, an old-fashioned man ill at home, thinks the nurse mistaken to keep both windows open, while Alice dreams of dances, beaux, and a life beyond her station.

Tarkington tells Alice's story with sympathy and irony, as she schemes, hopes, and learns the price of pretence. Her father's quiet heroism and her own growth give the novel its heart. Alice Adams, which won the Pulitzer Prize, remains a classic American novel of class, ambition, and a young woman's coming of age.
a-defence-of-poesie-and-poems:
Sir Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesie stands here in the 1891 Cassell edition, with a long introduction giving his life from his birth at Penshurst in 1554. Sidney wrote the essay to answer attacks on poetry in a puritan age. He argues that the poet teaches and delights better than the historian or the philosopher.

The essay ranges over epic, tragedy, comedy, and lyric, weighs the poets of Greece and Rome, and closes by cursing those who scorn the craft. Sidney's own poems follow, including sonnets that made him the model courtier-poet of Elizabeth's England. The pairing shows the critic and the poet in one short, brilliant career.
a-reading-of-life-with-other-poems:
George Meredith's verse volume, printed in London in 1901, takes its name from the long opening group of poems, A Reading of Life. The contents list pieces such as The Vital Choice, With the Huntress, With the Persuader, and The Test of Manhood. Meredith was better known as a novelist, but he prized his poems highly.

The poems weigh love, strength, regret, and man's place in nature, often in tight, demanding stanzas. Later pages hold Forest History, A Garden Idyl, and hexameter fragments retelling scenes from the Iliad, plus a piece drawn from the Provençal poem Mireio. The book rewards slow reading and a taste for thoughtful verse.
alice-adams:
Booth Tarkington's novel opens in the Adams home, where old Virgil Adams lies sick and quarrels with his nurse about night air. The story then turns to his daughter Alice. She is a young woman in a midwestern town. She longs for finer rooms, finer clothes, and a finer place in society than her family's money allows.

Alice and her mother scheme, pretend, and spend beyond their means to win the notice of a wealthy young man. A disastrous dinner party exposes the gap between the family's show and its truth. Tarkington treats Alice with both satire and pity, and the novel became one of his best known works.
anne-s-house-of-dreams:
Lucy Maud Montgomery opens this Anne novel in the garret of Green Gables, with Anne Shirley finishing with geometry for good and her wedding to Gilbert Blythe ahead. The contents list forty chapters. The couple's first home is a small house at Four Winds harbor, which Anne had dreamed of, and the book follows their first year of marriage there.

New neighbors fill the story. Captain Jim is the lighthouse keeper, with a life-book of sea tales to write down. Miss Cornelia Bryant is tart and kind. Leslie Moore is beautiful and trapped in a loveless marriage to a man lost in his mind. Joy and grief both visit the little house, including the loss of a first baby. The final chapters free Leslie, finish Captain Jim's book, and take Anne to a larger house.
aretaeus-extant-works-adams:
Francis Adams translated the Extant Works of Aretaeus the Cappadocian in 1856. Aretaeus practiced medicine around 150 CE in the Roman Empire. Posterity ranks him the finest clinical observer of antiquity.

His descriptions of diabetes, asthma, epilepsy, and tetanus remain classics. He watches symptoms closely and writes them down with literary power. Diabetes receives its classic portrait here, thirst and wasting included. Adams kept the exact Greek sense in careful English prose. Little is known of Aretaeus's life beyond these surviving books. Clinical medicine before the name existed is what his pages show. Physicians still quote his disease portraits with respect. His eye was sharp and his pen was just as sharp.
ballads-and-lyrics-of-old-france-with-ot:
Andrew Lang published Ballads and Lyrics of Old France in 1872, his first book, built largely on translations from French poets of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Charles d'Orleans opens the volume with spring songs and rondels. Francois Villon's Ballad of the Gibbet follows, then du Bellay, Remy Belleau, and Ronsard.

Lang renders roses, moons, dead ladies, and waking mistresses in the old fixed forms: ballade, rondel, and sonnet. His own poems close the collection, including a singer by the waterside drying her hands with willow leaves. The book helped revive English interest in the French lyric forms, and Lang's light, exact touch became his signature across a huge body of work.
canada-and-other-poems:
T. F. Young's Canada and Other Poems introduces its author's poetical attempts with great diffidence, and with a patriotic purpose. Young writes that, like Burns, he wished to do something for his country, and chose poetry as his method.

Canadian literature was in its infancy, Young argues, and must not remain so if Canada is to become a great nation. Literature, in his image, holds up a mirror to a nation's life and thought, one that heartens and ennobles its students. Young expects pedantic critics to fault his grammar and mechanics, and answers them with purpose rather than polish. Readers of early Canadian verse will find his ambition larger, and more interesting, than his finish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphabetic-ps:
Alphabetic psalms are so called because their verses, or parallel series, start with successive alphabet letters. Some formations are perfectly regular, others more or less defective. Among the regular ones are Psalms 110, 111, and 118. The praise of the strong woman in Proverbs 31:10-31 and Lamentations' first four chapters show a similar regular formation. Psalms 110 and 111 have twenty-two verses each, each verse beginning with the corresponding letter. Psalm 118 has twenty-two strophes of eight distichs each, each strophe built on one letter.

Proverbs 31:10 has twenty-two distichs, each beginning with the successive letter, and Lamentations 1, 2, and 4 each have twenty-two short strophes beginning with successive letters. In Lamentations 3, each letter begins three lines, making sixty-six lines in which each letter occurs three times as a line's initial. Defectively alphabetic psalms appear in Psalms 9, 24, 36, and 145, and the device also appears in other poetical portions of the Old Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burchard-of-w:
Burchard of Worms, bishop from 1000 to 1025, rebuilt his city, codified its laws, and gave clergy a canon-law manual used for over a century. Born of noble Hessian parents after mid-century, he studied at Coblenz, served Archbishop Willigis of Mainz as deacon, chamberlain, and city judge, and won Otto III's notice for discretion and fairness. Willigis made him Bishop of Worms in 1000 and raised him to priesthood and episcopate at Heiligenstadt.

He rebuilt Worms's walls, tore down Duke Otto's criminal refuge with Henry II's approval, and raised Saint Paul's monastery on its site. His sister Mathilda led a rebuilt women's community, and Saint Peter's cathedral rose again and was dedicated in 1016. Between 1023 and 1025 he issued the Leges et Statuta for Saint Peter's household to secure fair justice. His twenty-book Decretum, called Brocardus, gathered councils, popes, fathers, penitentials, and Scripture, and ruled clerical practice until Gratian about 1150.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-mus:
An entry on Christian museums, a term usually kept for collections rich in Christian objects from before the Middle Ages: sarcophagi, inscriptions, and minor arts. Such objects appear in many museums, but few houses devote themselves chiefly to them. Early humanist collections, such as the Medici at Florence, held medieval works for their art rather than their faith. Renaissance inscription collections ignored Christian texts until Bosio's discovery of the Roman catacombs drew collectors.

The Vatican's was the first Christian museum properly so called, founded by Benedict the Fourteenth as the Museum Christianum. With Marchi and De Rossi behind it, part of its holdings formed the Lateran Museum of 1854, which no other museum equals for Christian antiquities. Italy remains richest in such collections, from the Kircheriano and Saint Paul's to church atria and catacomb sites at Saint Domitilla and Saint Agnes, where inscriptions and sculptures still stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communicatio-:
Anthony Maas's entry explains communicatio idiomatum, a technical term of Incarnation theology, seeking its source and setting rules for its use. It means that properties of the Divine Word may be ascribed to the man Christ, and properties of the man Christ to the Word, an exchange Scripture and the Fathers allow. Its source is not a moral union, as Nestorians held, nor Christ's fullness of grace, nor the Word's right by creation.

Its base is one person subsisting in Christ's two natures. Three rules follow. Concrete terms stand for the person, so divine and human properties generally exchange. Abstract terms stand for their own nature and do not exchange. Care must guard both natures intact, even in negative sentences. By his divine nature Christ did not die, yet none may flatly say Christ did not die. A wider use in Eucharist theology closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congress-of-e:
Michael Ott's entry follows the Congress of Ems, a meeting at Bad-Ems near Coblenz in August 1786. Representatives of four German archbishops gathered: Erthal of Mainz, Maximilian Franz of Cologne, Clemens Wenceslaus of Trier, and Colloredo of Salzburg. Their purpose joined protest against papal interference in episcopal powers with fixing future archbishop-pontiff relations. Gallican principles on bishops and pope, spread in Germany by Hontheim, Trier's auxiliary, shaped their stance. His 1763 treatise, published as Febronius, argued episcopal rights against Roman claims.

Nuncio shifts framed the dispute, Bellisomi moving from Cologne to Lisbon while Pacca succeeded him at Cologne. The archbishops' Punctation assumed Christ gave apostles and successors unlimited binding and loosing power, treating papal prerogatives and reservations as concessions. Its articles reduced papal primacy toward the merely honorary and claimed independence from Rome. Archbishops insisted on their demands despite papal reply, though the reply still carried effect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foundling-asy:
Foundling asylums were institutions that took in infants whose parents could not or would not care for them, above all foundlings in the strict sense, babies deliberately abandoned. In pagan Greece and Rome, exposure of unwanted infants and direct infanticide had the sanction of law and opinion. Lycurgus and the Decemviri ordered deformed children killed, Aristotle defended exposure in his ideal state. Rome set aside two places for abandoning infants, most of whom were rescued only to become slaves.

Christian teaching that a child is sacred in itself, not a mere means to the state's ends, brought the first condemnation and the first organised rescue. Writers, priests, and bishops such as Lactantius, Tertullian, and Cyprian led it. The first recorded asylum was founded at Milan by Archpriest Datheus in 787, and Innocent III built one at Rome in 1198.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gradual-psalm:
The Gradual Psalms are fifteen psalms, Psalms 119 to 133 in the Vulgate numbering, 120 to 134 in Hebrew, bearing a Hebrew inscription rendered canticum graduum, a gradual canticle. The Authorized Version calls them songs of degrees and the Revised Version songs of ascents. A Catholic Encyclopedia article favors the pilgrim-song explanation.

Of the various conjectural explanations, the most probable treats them as psalms sung on the way up to the annual festivals in Jerusalem. The days on which they were formerly recited are still indicated in the Roman Breviary, but Saint Pius V removed the obligation of reciting them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hincmar-archb:
Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, was born in 806 and died at Épernay in 882. Descended from a distinguished West Frankish family, he was educated at St-Denis under Abbot Hilduin. He followed Hilduin to the court of Louis the Pious in 822, learned political and church administration at first hand, shared his master's banishment at Corvey, and returned with him to St-Denis.

King Charles the Bald took Hincmar into permanent service in 840, and he became the king's skilful counsellor in all matters. Raised to Reims in 845 at the Synod of Beauvais, he succeeded the deposed Ebbo in one of the great sees of the Frankish realm. The entry follows a statesman-prelate whose learning, loyalty, and long career shaped church and kingdom alike through decades of turmoil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-interims:
Temporary religious settlements imposed by Emperor Charles V on German Protestants are the subject here, from a Latin word meaning meanwhile. The first, the Interim of Ratisbon, closed the imperial diet on 29 July 1541 and built on a Catholic-Protestant conference that had agreed on justification and other points of doctrine. Its recess postponed a final settlement to the next council or diet.

Meanwhile Protestants were to hold to the agreed articles and go no further, church reform was to start under the bishops, the Peace of Nuremberg of 1532 was to stand. Monasteries, chapter houses, and church property were to stay intact. Protestants were also barred from winning new adherents. The entry shows an emperor buying time with a truce that settled nothing for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-interpretatio:
Sleep and dreaming have puzzled people since the earliest times, and this entry traces how that puzzlement became a theory of dreams. Waking minds can steer their thoughts. Sleepers can neither summon the dreams they want nor rule the dreams that come. That helplessness led early peoples to treat sleep as divine power's work and as something sacred. Arab reverence for a sleeping man may preserve a trace of that old view.

From that mystery grew the art of reading dreams as messages, and the entry follows dream lore through ancient and Christian sources, weighing what dreams can and cannot reveal. It treats dreaming as a human riddle rather than a settled science, inviting readers to see how theology, folk belief, and early psychology each tried to explain the night mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-adams:
James Adams was professor of humanities at St Omers. He was born in England in 1737 and died at Dublin on 6 December 1802. He became a Jesuit at Watten on 7 September 1756. He worked on the mission in England. He translated from French an early work on taking likenesses, titled Early Rules for Taking a Likeness, by Bonomaci.

The Royal Society of London thanked him for a treatise on English pronunciation. That work added appendices on dialects and a discussion defending Scots speech. He also composed a volume of Roman history. He planned a book on a tour through the Hebrides, which was never printed. The entry presents a Jesuit schoolman of letters, modest in output but noticed by London's learned society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-willem:
Pierre Willems was a Belgian scholar of Latin and Roman public law who taught at Louvain for more than thirty years. He was born at Maastricht in 1840 and studied at Louvain, Paris, Berlin, Utrecht, and Leyden. In 1865 he became professor of Latin philology, the study of language and literature, at Louvain.

His handbook of Roman public law, first issued in 1870 and running to seven editions, traces Roman institutions through monarchy, republic, and empire in clear, compact form. His three-volume study of the Roman Senate argued, against older views, that plebeians entered the Senate as former magistrates. Later scholars accepted that doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pius-bonifaci:
Pius Bonifacius Gams was a German Benedictine historian of the church, best known for two vast reference works. He was born at Mittelbuch in Württemberg in 1816 and studied at Tübingen. He was ordained in 1839 and taught philosophy and history at Hildesheim. In 1856 he took Benedictine vows at Saint Boniface's Abbey in Munich, adding Pius to his name.

His three-volume Church History of Spain of 1862 to 1879 is praised as conscientious and methodical, if too trusting of weak sources for the earliest period. More lasting is his Series of Bishops of the Catholic Church of 1873 to 1886, gathering the lists of bishops for every known see, ancient and modern, gaps and uncertain dates notwithstanding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalms:
The Book of Psalms, the first book of the Writings in the Hebrew Bible, receives a vast survey here. Its place in the canon varied across traditions. The Talmud puts Ruth before Psalms. Saint Jerome heads the Writings with Psalms in one letter, and with Job in another. Spanish Masoretic manuscripts begin with Chronicles. The Septuagint places Psalms first among the wisdom books. These shifting orders open a study of authorship, grouping and use.

Collections within the Psalter get close attention, including the hymns of the sons of Korah. Those psalms share a love of the Holy City, a yearning for public worship, a deep trust in God, and a simple, balanced poetic form. Their Messianic ideas and historical hints place them between Isaiah's days and the return from exile. Commentaries from many lands, down to 1909, close an entry that serves students of the Bible's prayer book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reims:
Reims is the archdiocese covering the district of Reims in the Marne and the whole department of Ardennes. Suppressed by the Concordat of 1802, which placed Reims under Meaux and Ardennes under Metz, it was restored in theory by the Concordat of 1817 and in fact in 1821. It gained Amiens and Soissons as suffragans in 1821 and Châlons and Beauvais in 1822. Its people, the Remi, had Durocortorum, the present Reims, as capital, and Caesar reduced them.

The entry follows Reims as a crowning and pilgrimage city. Kings came to touch for scrofula. Louis the Sixteenth sent the relics of Saint Marcoul to Saint-Remi instead of travelling. Louis the Eighteenth did not touch at all. Charles the Tenth touched the day after his consecration, softening the old formula to may God heal thee. Popes visited the city, and Carolingian rulers met there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-von-em:
Rudolf von Ems was a Middle High German epic poet of the thirteenth century, of whom almost nothing is known of his life. He served the Counts of Montfort. An anonymous continuator of his Weltchronik reports he died in Italy, probably with King Konrad IV, about 1254. He professed himself a follower of Gottfried von Strassburg, but his moralizing, didactic bent differs sharply from Gottfried's joyous sensualism.

In subject he favoured the learned, generally drawing from Latin sources. His earliest extant poem and one of his best, Der gute Gerhard, shows a humble Cologne merchant's simple piety shaming Emperor Otto's pharisaical ostentation. The didactic bent is conspicuous in Barlaam und Josaphat, a Christian legend rooted in Buddhist sources. His most ambitious works were the historical epics Alexander and Weltchronik, the latter a complete world history breaking off at Solomon's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synods-of-rei:
Reims hosted a long run of synods, and this entry lists them from the seventh century to the nineteenth. The first, said to have met under Archbishop Sonnatius between 624 and 630, is probably the same as Clichy in 626 or 627. Wulfar presided over a reform synod in 813, and Siguin of Sens deposed Archbishop Arnulf at St Basle in 991.

Leo IX held a reformatory synod in 1049. Legates excommunicated kings in 1115 and sought peace with Henry V in 1119. Later synods faced Gilbert de la Porée, urged crusade, fought Lutheran teaching, and enforced Trent. After a gap of nearly three centuries, Cardinal Gousset revived the series at Soissons, Amiens, and Reims between 1849 and 1857.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-adam:
John Adams was a priest martyred at Tyburn on 8 October 1586. Once a Protestant minister, he converted and went to Reims in 1579, where he was ordained priest. He came back to England in March 1581. Father William Warford, who knew him personally, pictured him as about forty, of average height, dark-bearded, sprightly, and black-eyed, a very good controversialist, straightforward, very pious, and above all a hard worker.

He laboured strenuously at Winchester and across Hampshire, helping many, especially among the poorer classes.
