Jailed in 1584, he was banished with seventy-two other priests in 1585, but he returned, was arrested again, and executed with John Lowe and Robert Dibdale. The entry preserves Warford's vivid portrait of a tireless missioner.
charmides-and-other-poems:
Oscar Wilde's Charmides and Other Poems reprints, in the 1913 Methuen selection, poems first gathered in 1881 and reprinted four times within two years. Charmides, a long narrative poem of a Greek youth who profanes Athena's statue, leads the volume. Requiescat, Wilde's tender elegy for his young sister, follows among Italian and classical pieces.

Sonnets address Milton, the Bulgarian massacre, Holy Week at Genoa, and the sale of Keats's love letters. Later sections gather the additional poems, including Ravenna and The Sphinx, mentioned in the edition's history. Readers can watch Wilde move from Pre-Raphaelite richness toward the ballad plainness of Reading Gaol, in a selection his literary executor shaped after his death.
confessions-and-criticisms:
Julian Hawthorne's Confessions and Criticisms gathers essays on fiction, American literature and art. Hawthorne opens with a preliminary confession: in 1869, aged about twenty-three, he sent two sonnets to the revived Putnam's Magazine while studying civil engineering at Dresden.

Later chapters treat novels and agnosticism, Americanism in fiction, literature for children, the moral aim in fiction, and the maker of many books. Essays on Mallock, Theodore Winthrop, Emerson as an American, modern magic, and American wild animals in art complete the volume. Readers interested in late nineteenth-century criticism will find Hawthorne candid, opinionated and often surprising.
discoveries-made-upon-men-and-matter-and:
Ben Jonson's Discoveries Made Upon Men and Matter gathers his prose notebook, printed here from the Cassell edition of 1892. Jonson called such collections a sylva, a wood of things and thoughts. The introduction explains the Latin joke: timber trees, promiscuously brought together. Some poems from his Underwoods accompany the prose.

The Discoveries record a great dramatist's judgments on poetry, manners, and his contemporaries. His remarks on Shakespeare, his friend and rival, are the most quoted pages. Maxims on language, imitation, and the poet's calling fill the rest. The introduction sketches Jonson's life from bricklayer's stepson to Camden's scholar at Westminster. Readers meet the learning behind the comedies: aphorisms, literary criticism, and self-portrait in one small volume. It is the nearest thing Jonson left to an autobiography of the mind.
doe-osti-2584729-scalable-algorithms-for: Inverse problems at scale got their algorithms, and this DOE report covers high-dimensional parameter spaces. The pages detail the scalable math. The computational scientists get their toolkit. The spaces were high-dimensional. The math was scalable. The scientists got toolkits.
doe-osti-2998338-radio-frequency-algorit: Radio frequency algorithms got their DOE write-up, and this text covers the RF math. The pages detail the methods. The engineers get their toolkit. The algorithms were radio frequency. The math was RF. The engineers got toolkits. The toolkit was engineer.
doe-osti-3001097-hybrid-bioenergy-and-hy: Bioenergy and hydropower got hybridized, and this DOE text leverages watershed biomass. The pages detail the systems findings. The energy folks get their option. The systems were hybrid. The option was energy. The findings were systems. The option was watershed.
doe-osti-3022998-georgetown-university-s: Written for a Georgetown graduate course in systems engineering, this report covers integration, verification, and validation — the discipline of making sure complex systems' parts work together and do what they were asked to do. It walks through the methods engineers use to test whole systems. A solid classroom treatment of a real-world engineering skill.
doe-osti-3023848-effects-of-velocity-on-: Radar waveforms got velocity-effected, and this DOE text studies the effects. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The waveforms were radar. The data were engineer. The velocity were effects. The radar were waveforms. The data were DOE.
doe-osti-3024022-exploring-enhancements-: Search UX got AI-explored, and this DOE text designs feedback explorations. The pages detail the enhancement findings. The computing folks get their data. The features were AI. The data were computing. The explorations were design. The AI were features.
doe-osti-3484481-modeling-combined-heat-: CHP got REopt-modeled, and this DOE slides cover combined heat power systems. The pages detail the modeling findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The REopt were CHP. The systems were power.
dreams:
Jerome K Jerome opens Dreams with his most extraordinary one: a theater cloak-room attendant demands he leave his legs behind before entering. Jerome confesses he objected less to the fee than to parting with his legs. The short sketches that follow keep that logic, in which dream absurdities proceed with perfect politeness.

Other dreams wander through spring woods and strange meetings, mixing nonsense with sudden tenderness about youth, love, and time passing. Jerome, famous for Three Men in a Boat, works here in miniature, letting a primrose or a west wind carry a whole reverie. The pieces are slight by design: humorous essays that use dreams to say what waking politeness would not.
dreams-and-days-poems:
George Parsons Lathrop's Dreams and Days gathers poems in five sections, from Strike Hands, Young Men! through The Bride of War to Arise, American! Lathrop's contents mix lyrics of nature and love with patriotic and memorial verse.

Songs of the bobolink, the song-sparrow and the phoebe-bird sit beside Grant's Dirge, Keenan's Charge, Gettysburg: A Battle Ode, and a rune of the rain breakers. Later poems include famine and harvest, the child's wish granted, and the flown soul. Readers of late nineteenth-century American verse will find Lathrop musical, earnest and deeply attached to home and country.
extracts-from-adam-s-diary-translated-fr:
Mark Twain pretends to translate Extracts from Adam's Diary from Adam's original hieroglyphics, in a note explaining that a friend printed a few incomplete copies years before. Monday opens the diary: a new creature with long hair is much in the way, always hanging around and following Adam about. He wishes it would stay with the other animals.

Adam names the animals, resents Eve's naming everything else, builds a shelter she improves, and slowly discovers affection under the comedy. At the catastrophe he admits he made one joke to himself at the fatal moment. Twain's shortest biblical squib became a classic; paired later with Eve's Diary, it lets Eden be retold by its most bewildered resident.
fleurs-de-lys-and-other-poems:
Arthur Weir's Fleurs de Lys and Other Poems gathers the Canadian poet's early verse, written between the ages of twenty and twenty-three. Weir chose the title for the Canadian verses at the front of the book, since their scenes belong to monarchical, fleur-de-lys-era France in Canada.

Many poems first appeared in the Montreal Star, the Toronto Week, the University Gazette and other papers, and their kindly reception led Weir to publish them in permanent form. He dedicates the volume to his parents, William and Elizabeth Somerville Weir, his most severe and kindly critics. Readers of early Canadian poetry will find Weir sincere, musical and proudly French-Canadian in sympathy.
forty-two-poems:
James Elroy Flecker published this, his gathering of forty-two poems, with J. M. Dent in 1911, four years before his early death. The hosted text comes from that edition. The opening piece, To a Poet a Thousand Years Hence, addresses a reader of the far future and asks what will survive of the writer.

Rioupéroux, named for the French alpine village where he had stayed, and The Town Without a Market show his eye for place. The War Song of the Saracens gives the collection its eastern colour, the strain that made his name. Flecker's verse is built on strict forms and gorgeously loaded lines, Persian and classical in its furniture. The book made his reputation while he was still a young consular official.
general-william-booth-enters-into-heaven:
Vachel Lindsay's title poem imagines General William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, marching into heaven at the head of his converted sinners. Bass drums and tambourines beat out the march, and the angels must answer the chorus. Lindsay wrote it to be chanted aloud, with performance directions in the margins. The poem made his name when it appeared.

Other pieces in the volume range from The Congo rhythms to Springfield poems, beggars, gamblers, and King Arthur's men returned. Lindsay mixes revival-meeting energy, vaudeville, and prairie populism into verse meant for the ear rather than the study. His work remains a landmark of American spoken-word poetry before that term existed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AdamsPerry_Vick: Vickie Adams worked in the Texas School Book Depository and became a witness in the Kennedy assassination. She said she ran down the building's back stairs moments after the shots, a point researchers have argued over ever since. This file holds the government material filed under her name in the assassination records. It is kept as issued, part of the witness paper trail that investigators of the case still work through today.
govdocs-archive_org-vaticancodesystems_V:
American codebreakers studied the Vatican's secret writing during the Second World War. The result was a 1944 cryptanalytic text on Vatican code systems, later reprinted by Aegean Park Press.

The study explains how papal codes were built and how an analyst should attack them: their alphabets, their habits, and their weak points. It treats the Holy See as what it was in wartime, a neutral power whose traffic every capital wanted to read. For students of cryptology, the manual is a rare look at professional codebreaking aimed at one of the world's oldest diplomatic services.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
When the United States negotiated with the Taliban, officials claimed the movement would break with al Qaeda. Newly Published Documents Cast Doubt on Claims Taliban Will Give Up al Qaeda tests that promise against the record.

The briefing book publishes documents that cut against the hopeful claim, drawn from the long history of ties between the two groups. Its method is the Archive's standard one: put the paper in public and let it argue. For readers following the Afghan settlement, the collection is a check on official optimism, grounded in documents rather than commentary.
grand-grimoire-1750-ms:
Before print fixed the Red Dragon's shape, the Grand Grimoire circulated in handwriting. This manuscript version dates to about 1750. It is an earlier redaction of the pact grimoire, textually distinct from the nineteenth-century printed editions that made the book famous across France.

The famous bargain with Lucifuge stands here in a less settled form. Scribes copied such books for buyers who could pay, changing details as they went. Comparing this draft-stage text with the printed Dragon shows the tradition in motion. The manuscript is the grimoire's own early state, before editors and printers froze it. Students of the French black books prize witnesses of exactly this kind.
heckewelder-history-manners-customs:
John Heckewelder was a Moravian missionary who spent forty years among Native peoples. His History, Manners, and Customs of the Indian Nations came out in 1818. The Lenape, or Delaware, stand at the center of his warm account.

Heckewelder describes councils, speech, war, and peace from long close contact. He defends his Native friends against the slurs of white writers. His respect and love for the people mark every chapter he wrote. Few early books on the Lenape are so humane or so full. Generations of readers have treated it as a classic of its kind.
helen-of-troy-and-other-poems:
Sara Teasdale's second book, Helen of Troy and Other Poems, appeared in New York in 1911. Its opening sequence gives voice to famous women of legend and literature: Helen, Beatrice, Sappho, Guenevere, and Erinna among them. Each speaks in the first person about love, beauty, and loss.

Shorter lyrics follow, grouped as love songs and single pieces with titles like Wild Asters, The Song Maker, and Buried Love. Teasdale's lines are musical, plain in diction, and exact about feeling, whether she writes of a rose, snow, or a lover gone. The volume helped establish her as a leading American lyric poet of her generation, admired for compression and song-like grace.
home-lyrics-a-book-of-poems:
H. S. Battersby's Home Lyrics, Volume Two, is a book of poems published after the author's death, as her children carried out her final wishes. Her children dedicate the volume to their mother's memory, praising a life consecrated to their happiness and welfare.

Contents include poems to a beloved son who died in April 1887, a little five-year-old, the angel on war, a Binghampton home, the Shaker girl, and an ice palace. Other pieces treat sunrise, love, Christmas morn, and a legend of old France. Readers of Victorian domestic verse will find Battersby tender, pious and deeply rooted in family life.
in-flanders-fields-and-other-poems:
John McCrae, a Canadian doctor serving at the front, wrote In Flanders Fields in May 1915, during the Second Battle of Ypres. A close friend had just been killed and buried among the poppies. The hosted volume came out in 1919, after McCrae's own death on duty. It gathers that poem with the rest of his verse. It also adds a memoir of him by Sir Andrew Macphail.

The title poem speaks in the voice of the dead. In Flanders fields the poppies blow between the crosses, row on row. Its call to take up the quarrel with the foe made the poppy the sign of remembrance across the Commonwealth. The other poems, many written in earlier, peaceful years, show the soldier-poet whole.
jack-winters-gridiron-chums:
Jack Winters' Gridiron Chums, by Mark Overton, is a school football story that opens with gruelling practice. Overton's contents introduce the boy who was in trouble and Big Bob, who confesses, before a friend in need and a message from Marshall set Jack and Joel investigating. Strange fruit for a tree to bear promises the mystery that school stories require alongside the sport.

The great game opens at chapter ten, with the struggle on the gridiron and glory enough for all. Then celebration turns dangerous: bed fire burns in Chester, Jack speaks for little Carl in the aftermath, and Big Bob brings news. Locking horns with Harmony, the rival school, builds to the great victory of the conclusion. Overton writes the American school story in its classic form, where football standings and moral standings are kept in the same ledger and settled on the same afternoon.
john-marr-and-other-poems:
John Marr and Other Poems is a book of poems by Herman Melville, with an introductory note by Henry Chapin. The 1922 edition lists three groups of verse. John Marr and Other Sailors opens the book, with Bridegroom Dick, Tom Deadlight, and Jack Roy. Sea Pieces follows, including The Haglets, The Maldive Shark, and Crossing the Tropics.

A third group draws poems from Timoleon, Melville's earlier verse book. Those pieces turn to art, Shelley's vision, and the age of the Antonines. The sea poems draw on Melville's own years as a sailor, the life behind his famous novels. Old sailors, storms, sharks, and far-off islands fill the pages. It is the late work of a novelist who ended as a poet.
laura-secord-the-heroine-of-1812-a-drama:
Sarah Anne Curzon wrote Laura Secord, the Heroine of 1812, as a drama with other poems. She dedicated the volume to all true Canadians. Its epigraphs praise bards who hand down heroes' names forever.

Laura Secord became famous for warning British forces during the War of 1812. Curzon turns that brave walk into stage drama. Other poems in the book widen its patriotic scope. The volume helped fix Secord's place in Canadian memory. It also shows a woman writer claiming national history as her subject. Curzon wrote as both poet and Canadian historian. Her Secord stands as a model of quiet courage under pressure.
lays-of-ancient-virginia-and-other-poems:
James Avis Bartley published Lays of Ancient Virginia at Richmond in 1855. Bartley came from Orange County, Virginia. He inscribed the volume to his father in a formal dedication.

A prefatory letter addresses the public directly and frankly. The poems look back to Virginia's early, colonial days. Local places, families, and memories supply their subjects. Bartley writes in the popular ballad style of his time. His book preserves a Virginian's pride in his state's past, just before the Civil War. Bartley's letter shows a young author anxious yet hopeful. Local readers were clearly the audience he wrote for first.
lays-of-the-scottish-cavaliers-and-other:
William Edmondstoune Aytoun published Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers in 1849. This volume reprints that first edition word for word. He dedicated it to the Earl of Eglinton and Winton.

Poems treat Edinburgh after Flodden and the execution of Montrose. Others sing of the Bruce's heart and the burial march of Dundee. The Widow of Glencoe and Charles Edward at Versailles follow. Aytoun mourns Scotland's Jacobite and royalist heroes in stately verse. Miscellaneous poems close a collection steeped in national memory. Aytoun helped edit Blackwood's Magazine in his career. Jacobite sympathy gave his verse a ready, loyal audience.
legends-tales-and-poems:
Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer's Legends, Tales and Poems appears here in a student edition. Everett Ward Olmsted of Cornell edited it with notes and vocabulary. An etching by B. Maura fronts the book.

Olmsted supplies a life of Bécquer before the works. Bécquer wrote romantic legends set in Spanish towns and ruins. Ghosts, doomed love, and holy places fill his short tales. His poems, the Rimas, made him Spain's beloved lyric poet. This edition helped American students read him in Spanish. Olmsted's vocabulary lists help with Bécquer's rich Spanish. Brief notes point out places, saints, and old customs.
life-s-enthusiasms:
David Starr Jordan, Stanford's president, published these essays in 1906. The American Unitarian Association issued the Boston edition. Jordan takes his text from Cherbuliez's novel about Samuel Brohl. The text urges laying up absurd enthusiasms in youth.

We lose many enthusiasms along life's journey, the passage warns. Without a stock, we reach the end with empty hearts. Jordan appeals for doing things because we love them. Good English, he adds, is life's most valuable habit of manners. Victor Cherbuliez's cynical story supplied Jordan's unlikely sermon text. Right words, discarded rivals, define good writing in his opening meditation.
london-films:
W. D. Howells gathers his London sketches under a film metaphor. Meteorological Emotions opens the contents list. Civic and social comparisons, mostly odious, follow wryly. Shows and side-shows of state bring ceremony into view.

Chapters enter the Commons gallery and Hampton Court. Henley Day and fishing for whitebait offer outdoor relief. American origins, northern and southern, occupy two later chapters. Howells watches fog, streets, and Londoners with an American's patience. Twice-seen sights and an afternoon at Hampton Court vary it. Some voluntary and involuntary sightseeing fills another chapter title.
love-at-arms:
Love-at-Arms is a swashbuckling romance by Rafael Sabatini. It claims to come from the chronicles of Urbino, in old Italy. The time is the rule of Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, duke and soldier. An Ariosto motto opens the tale: ladies, knights, arms, and loves.

The hero Francesco wins mercy and honor amid court plots. Monna Valentina brings love into the swordplay. Gian Maria, an amorous duke, and Gonzaga the insidious bring danger. There are wandering knights, a fool with sharp questions, and a rack. Sabatini keeps the action swift and the honor high. It is pure Renaissance adventure, told with dash.
love-or-fame-and-other-poems:
Love or Fame; and Other Poems is a verse collection by Fannie Isabelle Sherrick. Its title poem sets love against fame as life's two great prizes. The other poems share that earnest, sentimental tone. Sherrick writes of the heart's choices, hopes, and losses.

Her verses follow the popular American style of her day. They are musical, direct, and meant to be felt more than studied. Poems of ambition stand beside poems of devotion and home. The book pleased the general readers it was written for. It survives as a fair sample of period American poetry, sincere and songlike in manner.
main-street-and-other-poems:
Main Street, and Other Poems gathers verses by Joyce Kilmer, transcribed from the 1917 edition. Kilmer was an American poet of New Jersey and New York, born in 1886. The title poem walks a small town's chief street. Others sing of roofs, houses, and a snowman in the yard.

Many poems here are Catholic in feeling, like 'The Robe of Christ.' Others mourn fellow poets, Lionel Johnson and Gerard Hopkins among them. War enters with 'Mid-ocean in War-time' and a memorial to Rupert Brooke. 'The White Ships and the Red' closes on hospital ships. Kilmer himself died in France in 1918. His verse joins simple faith to plain American scenes.
many-kingdoms:
Many Kingdoms is a story collection by Elizabeth Garver Jordan, dated 1908. Its motto comes from Shakespeare: man's state, like a little kingdom, suffers insurrection. The first tale, 'Varick's Lady o' Dreams,' opens the book at night. Varick settles to sleep with a conscience absolutely untroubled.

Stories here include 'The Exorcism of Lily Bell' and 'His Boy.' 'The Simple Life of Genevieve Maud' and 'The Community's Sunbeam' lighten the tone. 'The Case of Katrina' and 'Bart Harrington, Genius' close the volume. Jordan wrote Tales of the Cloister and other popular books. Her kingdoms are the small worlds of ordinary hearts. Each tale turns on some inner rebellion or peace.
many-voices-poems:
Many Voices is a book of poems by E. Nesbit, in a 1922 Hutchinson edition. Nesbit dedicated it to her daughter-in-law, Gertrude Bland, at Romney that year. She is better known for her children's novels of magic and family. Poems here include 'The Return,' 'Questions,' and 'The Daisies.'

'The December Rose,' 'The Touchstone,' and 'The Stolen God' show her range. Songs, partings, and winter pieces fill the slim volume. Her verse is musical, direct, and quietly emotional. She writes of love, loss, and the gift of life. The poems suit grown readers more than children. They reveal the warm imagination behind her famous stories.
matthew-arnold-s-sohrab-and-rustum-and-o:
Justus Collins Castleman edited Matthew Arnold's Sohrab and Rustum in 1905. Castleman led the English work at a Milwaukee high school. His book adds an intro, notes, and a list of Arnold's works.

Sohrab and Rustum leads the tale poems in the contents. Saint Brandan, The Forsaken Merman, and Tristram and Iseult follow. The lyric part holds Dover Beach, Requiescat, and Lines Written in Kensington Gardens. Philomela, Human Life, and The Last Word show the range schools prized in Arnold. Consolation, A Dream, and Morality stand among the lyrics too. School notes help young readers through the tales' old world names.
maurine-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox published Maurine and Other Poems in a 1910 London edition. Gay and Hancock called it a popular edition, with many new poems. The long title poem fills the first half of the book.

Shorter poems follow, on God, dust, advice, and the past. Over the Banisters, The Two Glasses, and La Mort d'Amour stand in the list. A Christian's New Year prayer and a piece on God's measure add faith. Wilcox writes in smooth, warm verse meant to be read aloud and kept. Secrets, Applause, and The Story show her range of short themes. Faith, love, and loss return in poem after poem.
mazelli-and-other-poems:
George W. Sands called Mazelli, and Other Poems his first offering. His preface speaks to three topics: his friends, his book, and himself. Friends, he says, stood by him with sincere and strong help.

He lays the book at the shrine of his country's fame. Grief, he says, drove him to write when a glad life would not have. Mazelli runs through three cantos at the front of the book. A verse play, The Misanthrope Reclaimed, stands among the later pieces. He says men call such gifts genius, yet few would envy the pain. That stark note sets the mood for the verse that follows.
miscellaneous-poems:
George Crabbe's shorter narrative poems make up this collection. The best-known piece, Sir Eustace Grey, is set in a madhouse. A visitor and a physician walk the cells while a patient tells his story. The visitor begs to know no more, so torn is he by the scenes of woe.

Other poems include The Hall of Justice, Woman, and The Birth of Flattery. A set of Reflections closes the contents. Crabbe wrote about rural and broken lives with unsparing detail. Sir Eustace Grey turns that realism inward, onto a mind ruined by its own crimes and cares, displayed by the patient himself.
moral-emblems:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Moral Emblems began as a boy's game at Davos, in Switzerland. Lloyd Osbourne, Stevenson's stepson, tells the story in his preface. Osbourne was twelve, with a toy printing press, in a chalet above the snowbound village. Stevenson wrote the verses and cut the woodcuts for the little press.

This 1921 Chatto and Windus edition reprints those Davos Press pieces. Each emblem pairs a crude woodcut with a short moral poem. Osbourne describes winter nights, tobogganing, and his stepfather's workshop cheerfully. The verses are playful, catchy, and often comic, a craftsman's holiday work between the adventure novels that made Stevenson famous.
mountain-idylls-and-other-poems:
Alfred Castner King published this book of poems with Fleming H. Revell in 1901. His dedication explains the book's making. Friends helped arrange his manuscripts for publication after the shadows of hopeless blindness descended on him forever. A portrait of the blind poet fronts the volume.

Illustrations show the Colorado country his poems celebrate: Mount Wilson, the San Juan range, and Ouray. Uncompahgre Cañon and Emerald Lake appear among the plates. King's mountain idylls praise the high Rockies he could no longer see. Readers valued the poems as a blind man's memory of grandeur, kept in verse.
music-and-other-poems:
Henry Van Dyke dedicated this verse book to his son Tertius. Scribner's issued it in October 1904. The contents sort the poems into odes, sonnets, legends, and lyrics. Music, Peace, and God of the Open Air lead the odes.

Sonnets treat work, life, love, and a child in a garden. Lyrics range from A Mile with Me to Indian Summer. Van Dyke writes in a clear, songlike voice on faith and nature. His lines aim to lift and calm the reader. The book shows why he was among the most loved American poets of his day.
nala-and-damayanti-and-other-poems:
Henry Hart Milman turned Sanskrit poems into English verse for this book. Talboys issued it at Oxford in 1835. Milman was a minister and late Oxford professor of poetry. He inscribed the volume to his mother with warm thanks.

Her pleasure in the translations was his best reward, he writes. The title poem tells of Nala and Damayanti, famed lovers of Indian epic. Notes explain myths and hard points for English readers. Sanskrit spelling is kept as the old book had it. Milman's verse brought a great Sanskrit love tale to British readers who knew no word of the source.
nasa-tm-19640023916-meteorological-satel:
Herbert Butler of the Aeronomy and Meteorology Division at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this September 1964 report on weather satellite data systems. It deals with how data from weather satellites in orbit would be gathered and handled on the ground.

Butler lays out the data system as a working problem, not just a sensor problem. A satellite is useful only if its readings reach forecasters in a usable form. The report covers that ground side of the system, so readers see what early weather satellite work required beyond the spacecraft itself.
nasa-tm-19670027698-the-analysis-of-tops:
In September 1967, NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this paper on reading satellite radio echoes. It treats the analysis of topside ionograms, the echo traces a sounder records while looking down at the ionosphere from above it. The catalog record ties the work to Alouette II, a Canadian satellite that sounded the ionosphere from orbit.

The method at the center of the paper is called lamination, a layered way of converting echo traces into electron density profiles. Sections outline the concept, discuss how the method works, and then examine its errors frankly. Error sources include the selection of data points, the choice of lamination model, the importance of iteration, and the integration technique used. One section compares the approach against observations from actual Alouette II ionograms. An appendix supplies the formulas for group and refractive indices, including special cases near the reflection point.
nasa-tm-19680009613-kinetic-theory-of-in:
John C. Price wrote this theory paper in March 1968. It presents a kinetic theory of inhomogeneous systems, systems whose properties change from place to place. Kinetic theory tracks huge numbers of particles statistically instead of one by one. Most of its results then assumed an endless, uniform system. Real systems never quite match that picture.

Price notes that corrections built for uniform systems lose their range of validity as they grow more accurate. His theory instead treats the coupled equations of the various hierarchies as simultaneous equations in time. The solution proceeds by successive approximations rather than a power series expansion in a small parameter. The scheme suits the derivation of equations for non-uniform and force-driven systems, the kind actually met in experiments. Worked examples are given for two cases: a plasma and a Boltzmann gas.
nasa-tm-19680019447-manufacturing-engine:
Volume 1 of Marshall Space Flight Center's Research Achievements Review covers manufacturing engineering research, in a 1967 memorandum, TM X-53721. Building rockets at Marshall meant inventing new ways to join, weld, and check huge metal parts. The volume gathers that shop floor research in one survey, from cleaner work areas to welding in space.

Listed topics include contamination control, remote welding methods, and ways to copy weightlessness on the ground. Laser uses, buoyancy simulation, and electron beam welding in space also appear. One detailed section weighs older tracking tools, then presents camera guided arc welding. Its cameras follow tack welded joints so the weld head can steer itself along the seam.
nasa-tm-19700019377-solutions-of-two-hea:
Mark D. Ardema of NASA's Mission Analysis Division at Moffett Field, California, wrote this report in June 1970. It solves two heat conduction problems tied to hypersonic cruise aircraft. Such planes would burn liquid hydrogen and need insulation to shield their tanks and skin.

Ardema works out exact solutions for heat flow through insulation systems. He then turns them into a way to estimate how much the insulation would weigh. His numbers are checked against a step-by-step computer method. The abstract states that the two sets of results agree very well.
nasa-tm-19720011113-spacecraft-cryogenic:
Spacecraft Cryogenic Gas Storage Systems is a NASA working paper, numbered MSC-01506, from the Manned Spacecraft Center in 1971. It surveys how spacecraft store oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and helium as very cold liquids. Storing gases this way is attractive because liquids pack densely and rest at low pressure, so tanks can be smaller and lighter.

The contents compare storage techniques first: high-pressure systems, supercritical storage, and subcritical storage. Then come flown systems, the Gemini cryogenic system and the Apollo command and service module systems. Later sections describe a supercritical helium system with its ground support equipment, and the lunar module's helium tank. Concepts for later programs follow, including discrete-shield, liquid-shrouded, and single-wall tank designs, plus the associated technology behind them.
new-poems:
Francis Thompson's New Poems came out in London from Burns and Oates in 1907, in a third English edition. The contents divide the book into two named parts. The first, Sight and Insight, opens with The Mistress of Vision and Contemplation. By Reason of Thy Law and The Dread of Height follow.

An Orient Ode, New Year's Chimes, and Assumpta Maria sit in that first part too. The second part, A Narrow Vessel, turns to love and loss. A Girl's Sin is told first in her eyes, then in his. Love Declared, Penelope, and an epilogue close the book. Faith and love share Thompson's pages here.
oklahoma-and-other-poems:
Freeman Edwin Miller published Oklahoma and Other Poems in 1895. He taught English at the Oklahoma agricultural college. The book was printed in Buffalo, New York. Miller dedicated it to poet James Whitcomb Riley. The title poem honors the young Oklahoma Territory.

The hosted sample preserves the title pages and dedication. It gives no readable text of the poems themselves. Readers can confirm the author, date, and place from the sample. They cannot judge the verse from this sample alone. The book stands as early Oklahoma literary work. Charles Wells Moulton printed the volume for the author.
old-english-sports-pastimes-and-customs:
Peter Hampson Ditchfield first published this study in 1891. The pieces first ran in The Parish Magazine. Ditchfield was rector of Barkham and a history fellow. He describes holiday festivals month by month. Each month brings its own sports, games, and customs.

Ditchfield drew on older writers such as Strutt and Stow. He writes in simple language for village readers. He hopes to revive the best of old village life. Lost customs might return, he suggests, with care. The book preserves rural feasts that time was erasing. Parish readers first met these pieces as short magazine articles each month.
old-spookses-pass-malcolm-s-katie-and-ot:
Isabella Valancy Crawford wrote these narrative poems of Canada. She dedicated the volume to her uncle, a navy doctor. The title poem opens on Yaller Bull Flat at night. Three cowboys camp there with a large herd. The speaker praises their skill with rope and broncho.

The cowboys argue well but play poor hands at brains. Crawford writes in rough western dialect for that poem. Malcolm's Katie tells a backwoods love story in verse. Her verse glows with the energy of young Canada. She ranks among Canada's finest early poets.
on-the-king-s-service-inward-glimpses-of:
Innes Logan wrote this tribute to soldiers of the Great War. Logan served as chaplain to the forces for twenty months. His service ran from September 1914 to May 1916. Hodder and Stoughton published the book in 1917. He dedicates it to his wife at Braemar.

Chapter one asks why the first hundred thousand enlisted. Later scenes visit a sunny reinforcements camp. A man from Skye receives his own short portrait. Logan honors men with whom he served closely. The subtitle promises inward glimpses of men at arms. The book blends faith, grief, and quiet admiration.
our-profession-and-other-poems:
Jared Barhite, principal of the Third Ward Grammar School in Long Island City, New York, gathered Our Profession and Other Poems in 1895 from a quarter century of spare-time verse. His preface calls the poems vagrant pastimes: some had wandered far in print, others had never been seen by any eye but his. To call them home, introduce them to each other, and properly house them seemed a parental duty.

The title poem takes teaching itself as its theme. If any thought in the volume inspires others of the profession to feel the dignity and responsibility of the calling, Barhite writes, publication will not have been in vain. The book is a schoolmaster's testament: poetry as the record of an ordinary, earnest Victorian working life.
outlines-of-a-mechanical-theory-of-storm: Thomas Bassnett's Outlines of a Mechanical Theory of Storms is a work of weather theory for seamen. The hosted sample shows the transcriber's note and title page only. That title page makes large claims. The book contains the true law of lunar influence, it says. Practical instructions to the navigator follow from it. A sailor could calculate coming changes of wind and weather, for any day and any ocean. No theory text appears in the sample.
phantasmagoria-and-other-poems: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Phantasmagoria and Other Poems, the title pages and inscription verses of the 1911 Macmillan edition, with no poems visible. The title page names Lewis Carroll and illustrator Arthur B. Frost, and notes the book was first published in 1869. The inscription verses, addressed to a dear child in memory of golden summer hours, end by warning the rude scoffer not to deem such hours a waste of life.
pike-county-ballads-and-other-poems:
John Hay's Pike County Ballads and Other Poems gathers his verse under an introduction by Henry Morley. The contents run from rough frontier ballads to travel poems, love poems, and pieces on public events. They show the range Hay worked in as poet and statesman.

The Pike County Ballads themselves are Jim Bludso, Little Breeches, Banty Tim, The Mystery of Gilgal, and The Pledge at Spunky Point. They are written in plain, story-telling speech. Around them stand the Wanderlieder, with Sunrise in the Place de la Concorde and The Sphinx of the Tuileries. A New and Old section holds Miles Keogh's Horse, Christine, A Haunted Room, and Dreams. Readers meet both the river-country storyteller and the traveled man of letters.
playful-poems:
Playful Poems is a verse collection edited by Henry Morley, a professor of English at University College London. The book came out in London in 1891, in the Companion Poets series from George Routledge and Sons. Morley adds an introduction of his own at the front.

Most of the book gives old poems in modern dress. Chaucer's tales of Phoebus and the crow, Sir Thopas, and the Friar appear here, reshaped by hands such as Leigh Hunt and William Wordsworth. Poems by Gower and Lydgate follow, among them London Lickpenny. Leigh Hunt modernised two of the Chaucer pieces, as the contents page shows.
podcast-dannyjones-4YKsRXMT9Ms:
Street reporter Luke reports from a Tampa protest for Danny Jones's show. Armed officers stand close behind him as he works. He moves fast to ask marchers why they came.

One protester says she marches for Black lives and against police force. Others share anger, hope, and fear in short bursts. The tape captures noise, tension, and the feel of the street. No studio guest appears; the crowd itself is the subject. The episode preserves a raw slice of protest-era Florida as participants explained themselves in their own words. The fear near the police line feels close and real.
podcast-dannyjones-UpFqkpiOAMs:
Producer Dan Farah made a documentary on UFO disclosure featuring senior officials. He joins Danny Jones to argue that President Trump's rush to release UFO files has a real reason behind it. Farah lays that reason out. His account centers on what officials have told him privately about the phenomenon and the pressure building around it.

Farah speaks as a man who has sat with the generals and intelligence figures his film assembled, and he reports their seriousness as the story. Jones presses him on what disclosure would actually contain. The claims remain officials' alleged private views, unverifiable here, and Farah's presentation is preserved as such. Listeners following the disclosure saga get its best-connected advocate explaining the endgame he expects, and the political clock he says is driving it.
podcast-tuckercarlson-677g2SsetMs:
Economist Jeffrey Sachs warns Tucker Carlson about forces pushing President Trump toward war with Iran. Sachs, a Columbia professor and longtime UN adviser, has become a fierce critic of American foreign policy. He also addresses the Ukraine and Russia war and its latest escalation.

Sachs argues that a permanent war lobby in Washington steers presidents toward conflict. He traces the Ukraine war to NATO expansion and broken promises, as he sees it. Carlson asks what Trump can do to resist the pressure. Concerned viewers hear a veteran insider's warning from the edge of the establishment.
podcast-tuckercarlson-6gmdh5DxfMs:
Activist Charlie Kirk joins Tucker Carlson to discuss Christian values under attack, the death of JFK, and how Trump changed politics forever. Kirk founded Turning Point USA and built a youth movement on campuses. His youthful fire fills this talk with his mentor Carlson.

Kirk argues that faith is the front line of the country's cultural war. He shares his reading of the Kennedy assassination and the distrust it seeded. The pair trace how Trump remade the Republican Party in ways that cannot be undone. Young and faithful viewers get the activist's full take from a flagship conversation.
podcast-tuckercarlson-6kGowc9TTms:
Tucker Carlson recalls the day a candidate was shot in the face on camera. Five months later, he says, no true accounting has come. The shooter died, the world moved on, and the story vanished.

Federalist writer Sean Davis was on the case from the start. The title promises an update on the Trump shooting. It also charges that Congress refuses to probe for a reason. Davis and Carlson ask who the shooter was and how he got close. The episode demands answers that officials have not given. Silence from officials hangs over the whole talk.
poems:
Alan Seeger was an American poet from New York who died young in the First World War, and his Poems collects his verse with an introduction by William Archer. Seeger wrote lyrics, sonnets, and narrative pieces in a romantic style, drawn to beauty, love, and distant places. The volume preserves the whole range of a short career that ended in 1916.

Early pieces gathered as juvenilia include an ode to natural beauty, a deserted garden, and a poem on the torture of Cuauhtemoc, the Aztec ruler. Thirty sonnets form a central block, and other poems range from Paris scenes to a sultan's palace. Archer's introduction frames the work for readers meeting Seeger after his death in service. The collection stands as the main record of a poet often remembered for one famous war poem.
reflections-or-sentences-and-moral-maxim:
François, Duc de La Rochefoucauld, wrote the maxims gathered here, in an English version drawn from the editions of 1678 and 1827. J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell translated the book, adding an introduction, notes, and an account of the author and his times. Simpson Low of London issued it in 1871.

Quotations at the front set the tone: Swift held the maxims true to nature, and Montesquieu called them the proverbs of men of wit. The contents add three supplements of further maxims and reflections on various subjects. Rochefoucauld's short, sharp sentences on pride, love, and self-interest fill the book.
renascence-and-other-poems:
Edna St. Vincent Millay's poems are gathered here under the title of her long first piece, Renascence, whose opening line the contents quote: All I could see from where I stood. Interim follows, beginning The room is full of you, and The Suicide speaks in a curse against life. No year is printed on the opening pages.

God's World cries that the world cannot be held close enough, and Afternoon on a Hill promises gladness under the sky. Sorrow falls like ceaseless rain in one poem, while Ashes of Life and The Little Ghost turn to loss and haunting. Three Songs of Shattering close the list, with roses, birdsong, and dogwood blossoms as their images.
robert-louis-stevenson-an-elegy-and-othe:
Richard Le Gallienne published these poems, mainly personal, in 1895, the year given in Roman figures on the title page. He dedicates them lovingly to his dear mother and father. The elegy for Robert Louis Stevenson, who had lately died, leads the book and gives it its name.

An Ode to Spring, Tree-Worship, and A Ballad of London follow the elegy. Paris Day by Day is billed as a familiar epistle. Poems on Alfred Tennyson, Professor Minto, Omar Khayyam, and Mr. Gladstone's retirement show the set's range of persons. Natural Religion, Faith Reborn, Jenny Dead, My Books, and Mammon close a young poet's book of homage, faith, and song.
rose-and-roof-tree-poems: George Parsons Lathrop wrote Rose and Roof-Tree, a book of poems with a brief verse motto and a warm dedication to the woman the poems honor. A first group called Windfalls holds the title poem, Music of Growth, A Song Long Ago, Melancholy, and Contentment. Part First then lists nature poems such as An April Aria, The Bobolink, The Sun-Shower, June Longings, The Song-Sparrow, Fairhaven Bay, and Chant for Autumn.
secret-societies-a-discussion-of-their-c:
Rev. David MacDill, Jonathan Blanchard, and Edward Beecher joined in this attack on secret societies. A line from Ephesians, urging readers to shun dark works and rebuke them, fronts the book. MacDill's treatise leads, with six chapters on the character of such groups.

MacDill weighs their age, their secrecy, their oaths, and their claims, and finds each one wanting. Blanchard then asks plainly if Christians should join such groups at all. Beecher adds a report made to a church body in Illinois. Church readers of the day got a firm, Bible-based case against lodge membership and secret oaths.
sixteen-poems:
William Butler Yeats chose these sixteen poems by William Allingham for the Dun Emer Press at Dundrum in 1905. Contents open with Let Me Sing of What I Know and The Winding Banks of Erne. Fairy pieces follow: The Fairies, The Lepracaun or Fairy Shoemaker, and The Maids of Elfin Mere.

Allingham sings of his home ground at Belashanny, where he was bred and born, in the Erne song. Ballads, laments, and a ruined chapel round out the choice. Yeats, a fellow Irish poet, here lifts an older singer's best work into a fine small press book for a new age.
sketches-of-japanese-manners-and-customs:
J. M. W. Silver, a lieutenant of Royal Marines, published these sketches of Japanese manners and customs in London in 1867. Native drawings, copied in color lithography, picture the scenes. Silver collected the sketches during 1864 and 1865, while attached to the Royal Marine battalion serving in Japan.

Silver dedicates the book to Colonel Sir Edmund Saunderson Prideaux, a friend and companion in arms of Silver's late father. The sketches aim to clear up the social state of a distant and little-known people, Silver states. British readers met Japan through a young officer's eyes just before that country opened wide to the world.
sociology-and-modern-social-problems:
Charles A. Ellwood, who held the chair of sociology at the University of Missouri, wrote Sociology and Modern Social Problems as a short first text. His preface says the book suits schools that can give the subject brief time. It also suits courses that join sociology with live social problems, or tie it to a course on trade and wealth, and it fits extension courses and teachers' reading circles.

Ellwood teaches the plain rules of the field by close study of one case. Chapters I to VIII state the base rules and show them through the rise, growth, shape, and work of the family. Chapters IX to XV then take up set problems in the light of those rules. He stresses how to read the facts over the facts themselves, and adds a short list of English reading at the end of each chapter.
some-christian-convictions-a-practical-r: Henry Sloane Coffin, minister of the Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church and a teacher at Union Theological Seminary in New York, wrote Some Christian Convictions. Its sub-title calls the book a practical restatement in terms of present-day thinking. Yale University Press held the 1915 copyright, and printings ran through 1920. The contents open with an account of nineteenth-century thought that has shaped Christian belief, then chapters on religion and the Bible.
some-poems:
Henry Morley frames war poems by Sir Walter Scott in Some Poems. The Vision of Don Roderick leads the contents. The Field of Waterloo and The Dance of Death follow. Short pieces include Romance of Dunois and The Troubadour. Pibroch of Donald Dhu stands in the list as well. Morley says room was left for more verses than Colonel Hay's. Scott's poems were added to fill that room.

Scott wrote the first poem in 1811. The fight with Napoleon then raged in the Peninsula. James Ballantyne and Co. first printed it at Edinburgh. Scott made it for a fund to aid Portuguese sufferers. He gave it to John Whitmore and the fund's committee. The Field of Waterloo came in 1815. A thin haze of war hangs over the small book.
songs-of-labor-and-other-poems: Morris Rosenfeld wrote Songs of Labor and Other Poems. Rose Pastor Stokes turned the poems from the Yiddish. Helena Frank shared that work with her. The contents name In the Factory first. My Boy and The Nightingale to the Workman follow. Despair, From Dawn to Dawn, and The Candle Seller stand in the list. The Pale Operator and The Beggar Family appear as well. A Tree in the Ghetto comes near the end. The Jewish May and The Feast of Lights close the run of titles shown.
songs-sonnets-miscellaneous-poems:
Thomas Runciman's Songs, Sonnets and Miscellaneous Poems came out in 1922. The printing was a private one. A first note signed W. R. gives his life. Runciman was born in Northumberland in 1841. He died in London in 1909. His father was Walter Runciman of Dunbar. His mother was Jean Finlay. In youth he left the fine coast for school and work. Newcastle was his place of training. William Bell Scott taught him art for a time.

Runciman painted portraits and landscapes all his life. He loved the landscapes most, the note says. Shy of shows, he stayed little known. His first full show came after his death. Newcastle held it in 1911. His poems were never offered for sale. He wrote them for his own joy. A few fast friends and kin held copies. Some verses were found in letters after he died. His daughter Kate Runciman Sellers saved others from sketch books.
state-of-the-union-addresses-of-john-qui:
John Quincy Adams gives four yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 6, 1825, to December 2, 1828. Three stars part each address from the next. The first opens with a wide survey of the country. Its first feeling is thanks to the Giver of All Good. Health spread wide through the land draws that thanks. Plenty scattered over the land draws it as well.

Peace and calm mark the hour, Adams says. Peace holds with all nations of the earth. Calm holds among the folk at home. Rarely has the state of Christian nations shown such peace. Europe has known ten years of it, he notes. Its governments learn by degrees a hard lesson there. Their end is the happiness of the people. Power can be borne out only by its blessings. Force alone cannot justify its use among men.
sun-up-and-other-poems:
Lola Ridge's Sun-Up and Other Poems gathers free verse first printed in journals such as The New Republic, Poetry, Play-Boy, and others, which she thanks for leave to reprint. A dedication poem to her mother opens the book, cradling the speaker back into the darkness of half shapes and first beginnings.

The contents group the poems as Sun-Up, Monologues, and Windows. The monologues include Jaguar, Wild Duck, The Dream, Altitude, Comrades, Nocturne, and Cactus Seed. The windows look out on city life: Time-Stone, Train Window, Scandal, Electricity, Skyscrapers, and Wall Street at Night. Ridge writes in open, modern lines that move between nature, dream, and the hard modern city.
tales-of-ind-and-other-poems:
T. Ramakrishna published Tales of Ind and Other Poems in 1896 and gave the book to the memory of his young daughter Kamala. Verse tales sit beside shorter poems, among them Seeta and Rama, The Story of Prince Desing, The Story of Rudra, and Chandra.

One early poem honors Lord Tennyson and praises a good life led with care for how others see it. Other pieces draw on Indian myth, old kings, and a tale of famine. Readers get English verse shaped by Indian tales and loss, with grief for a child held close at the start.
tanakh-jps-1917-psalms:
Psalms is the great songbook of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English version. The set is split into books, and Book One opens with a blessing on the man who shuns the counsel of the wicked.

That man delights in God's law and thinks on it day and night, like a tree by streams that bears fruit in season. The wicked, by contrast, are chaff blown off by the wind. The next psalm turns to raging nations and kings who plot in vain. Readers get 150 songs of praise, grief, thanks, and trust, sung by Israel for ages and still central to Jewish and Christian worship.
tell-me-another-story-the-book-of-story-: Carolyn Sherwin Bailey made Tell Me Another Story for Milton Bradley Company in 1918. Its subtitle is The Book of Story Programs. The front pages thank many houses for tales lent to the book. They name The Country Cat by Grace McGowan Cooke. They name The Little Acorn by Lucy Wheelock. Tales by Selma Lagerlof from the Nils books are also named. The Bird and The Gray Hare come from Tolstoi's Long Exile. How Peter Rabbit Got His White Patch is named as well.
the-bakchesarian-fountain-and-other-poem:
William D. Lewis translated poems from Russian into English and dated his dedication at Philadelphia in July 1849. Chief among them is Alexander Pushkin's tale of the Tauride, rendered here under the spelling Pooshkeen. Lewis thanks Russian friends for kindness shown to him in their country in early life.

Giray, a khan, sits mute with downcast eyes while courtiers stand in silence around him. Grief and strong feeling mark his brow before he raises his head and signals them to leave. Shorter poems by other Russian authors follow the title piece, giving English readers a small selection of Russian verse in one volume.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-19-psa:
Psalms , from the King James Bible, opens with a blessed man who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly or sit with the scornful. His delight is in the law of the Lord, on which he meditates day and night.

He is compared to a tree planted by rivers, bringing fruit in season, with leaves that do not wither. The ungodly are chaff driven by wind and will not stand in judgment. Psalm two then asks why the heathen rage and kings take counsel against the Lord. Song, warning, and kingship open the Psalter.
the-bride-of-dreams:
Frederik van Eeden wrote The Bride of Dreams, in an authorized translation by Mellie von Auw, printed at the Plimpton Press in Norwood, Massachusetts. The first chapter draws near to a little city from the sea on a summer day. Only the tall, round clump of trees on the ramparts shows at first. Above it rises the old bell-tower, its dome-top a deep cobalt blue.

The town once had, in Holland's prime, a short dream of worldly grandeur. Gilded ships, fishing boats, and warships filled its harbor then. Its folk built fine houses with crow-stepped gables and filled them with rare goods, plate, and china. Cannon stood on the ramparts, and pride ran high. Now all that is long past.
the-chinese-nightingale-and-other-poems: Vachel Lindsay, the Illinois poet, published this verse volume with a dedication to the poet Sara Teasdale. Only the front matter and contents are present here. They record that Harriet Monroe gave the title poem the Levinson Prize as the best contribution to Poetry: A Magazine of Verse for 1915. Later sections gather poems on America watching the war from 1914 to 1917, peace appeals tied to Jane Addams at the Hague, and Tolstoi. No poem text follows.
the-coming-of-the-princess-and-other-poe:
Kate Seymour MacLean of Kingston, Ontario, gathered her poems here under the title The Coming of the Princess. G. Mercer Adam, editor of The Canadian Monthly, introduces the volume. He explains that MacLean asked him for a few words of preface, and that he had often placed her poems before lovers of verse in the Dominion.

Adam asks readers to receive the book as a child of the first winds and suns of a nation. He acts, he says, as foster father to the collection, and he praises its high and sustained excellence as a whole. The volume, in his framing, is a worthy addition to the poetical literature of a young country. That national claim matters: Canadian verse was then building its own shelf, and an editor's blessing helped a Kingston poet reach it.
the-congo-and-other-poems:
Vachel Lindsay of Illinois wrote the poems gathered here, first published in New York in September 1914. Harriet Monroe, editor of Poetry, supplies the introduction. A note explains that stage directions for poems meant to be read aloud, set beside the first line in print. Here they are placed on the line before and marked off, so readers can tell text from direction.

Monroe recalls that Poetry began in Chicago in the fall of 1912 and that Lindsay was one of its first finds. His General William Booth Enters into Heaven led the January 1913 issue. She praises his loyalty to the people of his own place and time, shaped by his wandering trips across the country.
the-culprit-fay-and-other-poems: Joseph Rodman Drake's The Culprit Fay and Other Poems was published in New York by George Dearborn in 1836, entered for copyright on October 31, 1835. The author's daughter inscribes the poems to her father's friend Fitz-Greene Halleck. An index lists the title poem and pieces such as To a Friend, Leon, Niagara, songs, lines written in a lady's album, and a piece called Hope. Only the front matter and that index are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-education-of-henry-adams:
Henry Adams's The Education of Henry Adams traces its author's life in chapter heads from Quincy in 1838 to a dynamic theory of history in 1904. The heads name Boston, Harvard College, Berlin, and Rome, then Treason, Diplomacy, and The Battle of the Rams for the Civil War years in London. Twenty Years After breaks the tale before Chicago, Silence, and The Dynamo and the Virgin.

Adams, great-grandson and grandson of presidents, writes of himself in the third person as a man unfit for his age. The book is a famed study of failure and force.
the-englishman-and-other-poems:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's The Englishman and Other Poems, in a 1912 London printing, opens with The Queen's Last Ride, writ on the day of Queen Victoria's funeral. The poem bids the city hang its carriage-way with purple, bar work as she passes, and let army and navy lead while kings ride behind, a humble band. Heads must bare as the great coach rolls by.

Wilcox wrote verse that plain folk kept by heart. Pageant, grief, and pride fill this first piece. The book shows her gift at full stretch: strong rhyme, clear feeling, and lines made to be quoted.
the-feast-of-the-virgins-and-other-poems: H. L. Gordon wrote The Feast of the Virgins and Other Poems, entered at Washington in 1891. Only the front matter and table of contents are present here. The list names many short poems. Among them stand Address to the Flag and Christmas Eve. One marks Gettysburg and the charge of the First Minnesota. One marks the charge of Fremont's Body-Guard. Heloise, Hope, and a run of songs and tributes fill out the list. The set is a book of patriotic and sentimental verse.
the-formation-of-vegetable-mould-through:
Charles Darwin wrote The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms as his last book, a study of how worms make soil. This printing of 1904 marks the thirteenth thousand.

Darwin reports years of close watching: worms live long under water, roam by night, lack eyes yet sense light, hear nothing, and feel shakes and touch. He tells what they eat, how they digest leaves, and how chalk glands work. Inch by inch, worms pass soil through their bodies, bury stones and ruins, and build the fine mould that feeds plants. A small beast, he shows, can shape the face of the land.
the-ghetto-and-other-poems: Lola Ridge wrote The Ghetto and the poems gathered with it, giving the book to the American people with a stark verse welcome. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The contents name The Ghetto, Manhattan, Broadway, Flotsam, Spring, The Song of Iron, and Frank Little at Calvary, which shows a book of city poems on work, crowds, and the poor. No poem text appears in these opening pages, so the verse cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-habitant-and-other-french-canadian-p: William Henry Drummond, M.D., wrote the poems named on the title page, with an introduction by Louis Frechette and pictures by Frederick Simpson Coburn. The contents list dialect pieces such as De Habitant, The Wreck of the Julie Plante, Le Vieux Temps, De Papineau Gun, How Bateese Came Home, and De Nice Leetle Canadienne. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-hundred-best-english-poems:
Adam L. Gowans selected the poems in this anthology. Thomas Y. Crowell and Company published it in New York in 1904. Gowans dedicated it to James Fitzmaurice-Kelly. His prefatory note is disarmingly honest. He admits the title's selling power helped decide him. No single selector could truly earn that title. Only a vote of qualified poetry lovers could settle it. Such a vote is of course impossible.

Within those limits he claims an honest attempt. Every poem included is a gem, he asserts. None can be read too often. Each should be known by heart. Every lover of good literature deserves that inner store. He took great care with the texts. One firm line governed the choices. No poems by living authors appear. A portrait of Tennyson fronts the volume.
the-kings-and-queens-of-england-with-oth:
Mary Ann H. T. Bigelow published these verses in 1853. She printed them for the author. She inscribed them to her husband. He was the companion of her youth, middle age, and declining years. Her inscription apologizes in advance. The kings and queens were hastily written, she says. Impulse of the moment drove them. They served her own entertainment and her youngest grand-daughter's. Printing them was never in her mind.

Her preface asks friends' indulgence for many defects. She was sixty years old when she began rhyming, she notes. It was by way of experiment. The poems were meant only to visit a few friends. Her eyes made dressing the royal figures properly hazardous. What survives is a family's keepsake. A grandmother turned England's whole line of monarchs into familiar verse. Careless style and all, her children asked for it.
the-lonely-dancer-and-other-poems:
Richard Le Gallienne published The Lonely Dancer and Other Poems in 1913, with a frontispiece portrait by Irma Le Gallienne. The book opens with a sonnet addressed to Irma. In it, Time the bandit has locked away fair women dead, old friendships, and noble dreams. Yet all that loss seems small when the poet turns to her. He fills his last shrine with her light and incense. The contents begin a section under the title poem's name, starting with Flos Aevorum and a run of quoted first lines.

Those lines speak of love and longing: all the words in all the world, the afternoon lonely for a face, and thoughts before a sunlit twentieth year. Readers meet a lyric poet writing of love, loss, and time.
the-lutherans-of-new-york-their-story-an: George U. Wenner, pastor of Christ Church, wrote The Lutherans of New York: Their Story and Their Problems, published in New York by the Petersfield Press in 1918. What is present stops at the title page and contents; the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents divide the story by periods, from the seventeenth century (1648–1700) through 1900–1918, then turn to problems: the problem of synods, of language, of membership, and of religious education. Wenner dedicated the book to the Lutherans of New York in the twentieth century.
the-madman-his-parables-and-poems:
Kahlil Gibran's The Madman: His Parables and Poems opens with the narrator explaining how he became a madman. One day he woke from a deep sleep and found all his masks stolen, the seven masks he had fashioned and worn in seven lives. He ran maskless through the crowded streets shouting after the thieves, while men and women laughed at him or ran home in fear.

When a youth cried that he was a madman, the sun kissed his naked face for the first time, and he blessed the thieves who stole his masks. In madness, he says, he found freedom and safety, the freedom of loneliness and safety from being understood. A following piece, God, climbs a holy mountain across thousands of years, addressing God as Master, then Creator, then Father, and receiving no answer.
the-miracle-and-other-poems: Virna Sheard published The Miracle and Other Poems in 1913. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. Sheard dedicated the book to her brother Eldridge Stanton, junior, who died at Niagara on February 4, 1912, and added a short verse refusing tears for his brave death. The contents list seasonal and devotional lyrics: When April Comes, Christmas, The Heart Courageous, A Southern Lullaby, Hallowe'en, and The Rover among them.
the-mountain-spring-and-other-poems:
Only title page, dedication, and contents are present here for The Mountain Spring and Other Poems by Nannie R. Glass, published in Boston by Sherman, French and Company in 1913, so none of the poems appear. Glass dedicates the little book to her parents' memory, praising how they kept their altar fires burning.

Fifteen poems are listed. The Mountain Spring heads the contents, followed by Go Wander, Love, The Lilies, and Tell Peter. The Sleet, Answered, Alone, No Other, and Wealth come next. The Captives, The Living Water, Jesus Intercedes, Eve's Flowers, and Come Unto Me close the list, its titles turning steadily toward devotional subjects.
the-new-penelope-and-other-stories-and-p:
Mrs. Frances Fuller Victor's The New Penelope and Other Stories and Poems was printed at San Francisco by A. L. Bancroft and Company in 1877, with copyright held by Victor herself. Her preface, dated from Portland in August 1877, explains the collection. Its sketches of Pacific Coast life had appeared over time in the Overland Monthly. Other Western magazines printed some too. Their merit, she hopes, lies in picturing border life with the charm of newness.

The poems, by contrast, were written at all periods of her life and cannot be called peculiarly Western. They embody feelings that all hearts share, East or West, and she dedicates them to her friends on the Pacific Coast, most especially in Oregon. Contents begin with the title story, The New Penelope, followed by A Curious Interview and Mr. Ela's Story.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: Poems of the Class of '29 (1851 to 1889) form this section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes. A bracketed note calls the file Volume 2 of the 1893 three-volume set, as several sibling sections are called. Here only the title and contents appear; the poems themselves are absent. Titles include Bill and Joe, The Old Man Dreams, Mare Rubrum, and The Boys. A Voice of the Loyal North appears too. Later entries name Sherman's in Savannah, The Last Survivor, a class-meeting hymn, and a tribute to Benjamin Peirce.

Poems drawn from the three Breakfast-Table books form this section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes. A bracketed note calls the file Volume 2 of the 1893 three-volume set. From The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, 1857 to 1858, come The Chambered Nautilus, Sun and Shadow, and Contentment. The Deacon's Masterpiece, or the Wonderful One-Hoss Shay, comes from there too. The Professor at the Breakfast-Table contributes Under the Violets, a Hymn of Trust, and Robinson of Leyden.

The Poet at the Breakfast-Table, 1871 to 1872, adds Homesick in Heaven, Fantasia, and Aunt Tabitha. An epilogue to the whole Breakfast-Table series follows. The section then opens its first poem, The Chambered Nautilus. Holmes figures the shell as a ship of pearl sailing the unshadowed main, in the best known of all his lyrics.

Poems from Over the Teacups form this section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes. A bracketed note calls the file Volume 3 of the 1893 three-volume set. The verse list includes a piece to the eleven ladies who gave Holmes a silver loving cup. The Broomstick Train, or the Return of the Witches, appears, and At the Turn of the Road. Readings over the teacups follow, built on secrets: the banker's, the exile's, the lover's, the statesman's, and the mother's. The secret of the stars closes the set.

The opening poem answers the gift of that cup, presented on August 29, 1889. Who gave it, the verse asks. It answers that the secret cannot be stolen from the brimming flood. No mortal eye shall read the names enrolled below until the bowl is emptied. Only then is the red throat of thirst cooled.
the-ride-to-the-lady-and-other-poems: Helen Gray Cone published her poems in 1891. The title ride leads the volume. A first guest and a silence follow it. An arraignment and a going out of the tide come next. King Raedwald and Ivo of Chartres stand in the list. Madonna Pia and a story of the Orient appear there too. A resurrection, a trumpeter, and comrades follow. A house of hate closes the opening list. Only the title page is present here. The opening of the contents list appears with it. The poems themselves do not appear.
the-rowley-poems:
Thomas Chatterton's Rowley Poems are reprinted here from Tyrwhitt's third edition. Maurice Evan Hare edited the volume and wrote its introduction. It is dated 1911. The contents promise a section on Chatterton's life and death. Other sections treat the value of the poems. A bibliography, notes, and an appendix on the Rowley controversy follow.

Hare begins with Chatterton's birth in Bristol. The date was November 20, 1752. His father, also Thomas, had died three months earlier. The elder Chatterton was a subchanter in Bristol Cathedral. He also kept a local free school. Hare describes his fondness for reading and music. He collected Roman coins and reportedly studied magic. His source for magic was Cornelius Agrippa.
the-secret-of-dreams:
Yacki Raizizun, Ph. D., wrote The Secret of Dreams, priced at fifty cents. Its contents list three parts. They are The Dreamer, Varieties of Dreams, and How to Evolve the Large Consciousness. The opening section is headed simply Dreams.

Everybody dreams, Raizizun begins, but few value the phenomena of sleep. Readers must first drop materialistic ideas of what man is, he says. The physical man is no more the man than his coat. He is only an instrument for the real inner man, or soul. Dreams afford a separation of soul and body, he argues. That separation comes by natural sleep, by induced sleep such as hypnotism, or by death. In sleep the link is only released, while in death it breaks. The real man then functions in his astral body.
the-seven-conundrums: E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Seven Conundrums was published at Toronto by McClelland and Stewart in 1923. Little, Brown and Company held the copyright. Wallace Morgan supplied the illustrations. A frontispiece caption quotes a woman whispering that others will know from whom a rose comes. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. An introduction comes first, the list says. The Compact, beginning at page three, follows it. Conundrum number one comes next. No story text itself appears here.
the-sylphs-of-the-season-with-other-poem:
W. Allston's poems are gathered here under the title poem, a poet's dream. Companions include The Two Pointers and The Paint King. Sonnets treat works by Michelangelo, Raphael, Rembrandt, and Tibaldi. Ballads such as The Mad Lover and Will, the Maniac close the company. A prefatory note to the title poem answers an objection in advance. Some images in it do not belong wholly to the season described, the objector says.

Allston explains that he chose and arranged his images by the season of their greatest impression in his own experience. The running brook is by no means spring's alone. It belongs there all the same. Its motion and seeming joy image the earth's renewal after winter. The placid lake is assigned to summer by the same rule.
the-threshold-grace-meditations-in-the-p:
Percy C. Ainsworth's Threshold Grace gathers meditations on the Psalms first printed in the Methodist Times and reprinted here after his brief ministry ended. A prefatory note by A. K. S. hopes the volume finds a place in the devotional literature people turn to in the quiet hour. The contents list eleven meditations, from The Habit of Faith and Eyes and Feet to A Plea for Tears, Haunted Hours, and The Wings of the Dove.

The first meditation takes its text from Psalm 121: the Lord shall keep thy going out and thy coming in for evermore. Ainsworth calls that old Hebrew phrase a picture of life whose symbolism covers our whole experience. His gentle, literary devotion suits private reading, and the posthumous framing gives these short pieces the weight of a young minister's legacy.
the-tongues-of-toil-and-other-poems:
William Francis Barnard's Tongues of Toil and Other Poems, issued by the Justice Publishing Company of Pittsburgh, opens with its title poem speaking in the voice of labour itself. The men of sinewed hands, acclaimed by earth and seas, announce that they made the lords and gathered their spoil. Now the power of the masters falls at last, and a million slaves mass beneath western skies and eastern dawns. The poem challenges the few who stand enthroned at the gates of trade.

Barnard's workers recall serving as fools when time was young, glad of niggard boons, and forbear no longer. His verse belongs to the labour protest poetry of its era, direct, biblical, and unafraid of revolution. Readers meeting the title poem meet the whole book's argument: the tongues of toil have found one voice, and it is speaking to the strong men of all the world.
the-victories-of-love-and-other-poems: Coventry Patmore's Victories of Love appeared in Cassell's National Library in an 1888 edition from Cassell and Company. The contents list eleven poems, including Amelia, The Azalea, Departure, The Toys, If I Were Dead, and Sponsa Dei. Only the contents and a short introduction are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. The introducer, signing H. M., says another volume from the singer of The Angel in the House needs no introduction. Patmore is praised there as a clear singer of household love.
the-wild-knight-and-other-poems:
Gilbert Chesterton published The Wild Knight and Other Poems in 1900, when he still spelled his first name in full on the title page. A short note thanks the editors of the Outlook and the Speaker for permission to reprint many of the poems. Chesterton says the pieces were selected and arranged for unity of spirit rather than unity of time or value, and that many are juvenile.

The pages present here give that note and the start of a contents list, so the poems themselves do not appear. Early titles include By the Babe Unborn, The World's Lover, The Skeleton, A Chord of Colour, The Happy Man, and The Unpardonable Sin. The Donkey and Ecclesiastes appear among the visible entries.
the-world-english-bible-web-psalms:
Psalms, book nineteen in the World English Bible, opens with a blessing on the righteous. That person avoids the counsel of the wicked. He does not sit with scoffers either. His delight rests in God's law instead. He meditates on it day and night. The image is a tree planted beside streams.

Such a tree bears fruit in season and never withers. The wicked, by contrast, become wind-blown chaff. They cannot stand in the judgment, the psalm warns. Psalm two then asks why nations rage. Kings conspire against God and his anointed. Poetry for every grief and joy fills the 150 songs ahead.
tibullus-elegies-williams:
Tibullus, a Roman knight of the Augustan age, wrote love elegies that prize the quiet farm over the camp and the court. Theodore Chickering Williams turned the whole Corpus Tibullianum into English verse. The four books gather poems by Tibullus and by hands in his circle.

Delia rules the first book and Nemesis the second, while the poet dreams of a small farm and a faithful hearth. Later books sing of Messalla, his patron, and of Sulpicia, a woman poet of the house. Tibullus is the soft third voice of Latin love elegy, beside Propertius and Ovid. His longing for the countryside still reads fresh.
trees-and-other-poems:
Joyce Kilmer's Trees and Other Poems, in the edition of 1914, gathers verse first printed in various periodicals. A biographical note gives Kilmer's dates as 1886 to 1918 and names him an American poet of New Jersey and New York. An epigraph from Coventry Patmore sets a humble tone for the collection.

Kilmer dedicates the book to his mother in a sonnet. He recalls earning her praise as a schoolboy for halting verse and crude stories. Her smile, he writes, turns his dross to gold. The contents list The Twelve-Forty-Five, Pennies, Stars, and Old Poets beside the title poem Trees, the lyric that made his name.
war-time-financial-problems: Hartley Withers wrote War-Time Financial Problems, a guide to money in wartime. Pages present here hold his name and the book's title, followed by a publisher's list of his other works with press praise. The text itself is not shown. The list names The Business of Finance, Our Money and the State, and Stocks and Shares. Money Changing and The Meaning of Money follow. Review lines from the Financial Times and the Morning Post praise his gift for smoothing a thorny path for general readers.
yorkshire-dialect-poems-1673-1915-and-tr: F. W. Moorman, professor of English at Leeds, compiled these Yorkshire dialect poems spanning 1673 to 1915. The volume appeared for the Yorkshire Dialect Society in 1916 and 1917. Moorman dedicated it to Yorkshiremen serving in trench or on battleship. Pages present here hold the title page and the start of a contents list. Early entries name an awd wife dialogue, Henry Carey's Honest Yorkshireman, and Thomas Browne songs. The poems themselves do not appear in these pages.
young-adventure-a-book-of-poems:
Stephen Vincent Benet published this first book of poems in 1918. A dedication in verse gives the rhymes to a childhood hero figure. Benet calls his friend Perseus, D'Artagnan, and Lancelot in one breath. Chauncey Brewster Tinker wrote the foreword. Tinker opens by saying the old civilisation seems to crumble underfoot. Poetry then returns like a dear memory, he writes.

Some poems had already run in periodicals. Benet was barely twenty when the volume appeared. Readers get youthful, bookish verse full of romance and heroes. The foreword frames the poems as a young man's answer to a world at war.
